docs.title: How to use claude-cowork-code
docs.text:
🌐 Published at nithun.github.io/claude-cowork-code-guide

This is the team handbook for the Cowork + Claude Code way of building software at TAP. It assumes nothing about Frappe — the method works on any stack. Where TAP LMS is used as an example, it's labelled.

docs.title: What this gives you
docs.text:
• Cowork does the thinking on paper — ideas, specs, change requests, reviews.
  • Claude Code does the building — code, tests, running things, maintaining the agent layer.
  • A set of subagents that each own one step (write the PRD, scope the change, build it, review it, test it), and a memory + retrospective loop that turns recurring mistakes into rules so the project gets more correct over time.

The whole thing is held together by one rule: two tools, one folder, never the same file at once. Handoffs go through named files, not chat.

docs.title: Pick your path
docs.text: You are… Read New to the system, setting it up Getting started Standing this up on a new Frappe app (common case) Adopt it for a new Frappe app Standing this up on a non-Frappe stack Adopt it for a new project In product — have an idea or a bug to report Product playbook In engineering — building or changing a feature Engineering playbook Writing Frappe code — need the patterns + landmines Frappe reference skills Wanting to understand why it's built this way Methodology Curious how the agents get better over time How the system improves itself Publishing these docs Publishing

docs.title: Reading order (first time)
docs.text:
1. Getting started — install the two tools, open a project, confirm it's wired.
  2. Methodology — the mental model: the two-tool rule, the agents, the memory loop. ~10 min. (The loop in depth: How the system improves itself.)
  3. Then whichever playbook matches your role (product or engineering).
  4. When you start a new repo: a Frappe app (the common case) or a different stack. Writing Frappe code? Keep the Frappe reference skills handy.

docs.title: The shape of a day
docs.text:
Cowork:  "Write a PRD for X"           → docs/prds/PRD-NNN.md
Cowork:  "Write a CR for behavior Y"   → docs/change-requests/CR-NNN.md
  (you review and approve the doc)
Code:    "Implement CR-NNN"            → code + tests, then review + test run
  (you copy to the running env, commit, deploy)
Code:    "Run retrospective"           → the system learns from the work

Same loop on every project. The agents and skills change per stack; the loop doesn't.

docs.title: Adopt it for a new project
docs.text:
You're starting a new TAP feature in its own repo, or a brand-new microservice (FastAPI, Node, a data pipeline). This page shows how to stand up the Cowork + Claude Code system there.

Is your new project a Frappe app? That's the common case at TAP, and it has a shortcut — you reuse the existing frappe-* skills and Frappe-aware agents directly instead of regenerating them. Go to Adopt it for a new Frappe app. This page covers the general (non-Frappe / different-stack) path.

docs.title: The model: bootstrap fresh, don't fork
docs.text:
Do not copy claude-cowork-code into your new repo. Most of what's here is TAP-LMS-specific — the frappe-* skills, the Frappe/Postgres rules baked into feature-builder / code-reviewer / test-runner, the accumulated lessons. Dragging those into a FastAPI service is pure noise.

Instead, run four bootstrap prompts in your new repo. They make Claude Code discover your stack and generate an agent layer that fits it. The methodology comes over; the Frappe baggage doesn't. The prompts live in docs/cowork-bootstrap.md — copy them from there; this page is the orientation around them.

Why discovery beats a template: a template bakes in assumptions (build command, test runner, language). Discovery asks. That's what makes the same four prompts work for a Frappe app, a FastAPI service, and a Node API without edits.

docs.title: Before you start — three decisions
docs.text:
Prompt 0 will ask you these. Decide in advance:

Decision Recommended default Why Where is the agent layer tracked? Inside the new code repo Simplest. Use a separate repo only if the code repo must stay deployable/clean. Self-improvement autonomy Proposal-only for ~the first month The retrospective suggests memory/agent edits; you apply the good ones. Graduate to closed-loop once proposals are consistently good. Which agents The full 8 only if the project warrants it A small service can start with feature-builder + code-reviewer + test-runner + retrospective and add prd-author / change-requirement / architecture-reviewer / task-manager when the planning load shows up.

docs.title: The four prompts
docs.text:
Open Claude Code in the new repo and paste them in order, waiting for each to finish.

# Prompt What it does Writes anything? 0 Discovery Inspects stack, build/test commands, git root, any existing .claude/, and whether code runs from a separate location (symlink needed?). Then proposes a plan and asks the three decisions above. No — read-only 1 Scaffold Creates CLAUDE.md, WORKFLOW.md, .claude/agents/ (each with an ## INVARIANTS (do not edit) fence), and .claude/memory/ (lessons, patterns, circuit-breaker, empty logs). Uses the build/test commands it discovered. Yes — commits the layer 2 Retrospective agent Adds .claude/agents/retrospective.md in proposal-only mode, with its own INVARIANTS (it can never weaken them, even on itself). Yes 3 Seed + verify Drafts initial lessons from your git history (you approve), then dry-runs the retrospective in report-only mode and verifies the whole setup. Proposes, then applies what you confirm

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
After the four prompts your new repo has:

your-service/
├── CLAUDE.md            ← project context: YOUR stack, build/test commands, conventions
├── WORKFLOW.md          ← the path-per-task-type map, same shape as TAP's
├── .claude/
│   ├── agents/          ← agents generated for YOUR stack
│   └── memory/          ← lessons.md, patterns.md, circuit-breaker.json, *.jsonl
└── (your code)

No skills/frappe-*, no TAP lessons — a clean layer that knows your build and test commands.

docs.title: What carries over vs. what gets regenerated
docs.text:
Carries over near-verbatim Regenerated for your stack prd-author — writing PRDs/BRs is stack-agnostic feature-builder — knows your language, framework, test idioms change-requirement — CR scoping is universal code-reviewer — checks your stack's footguns (not Postgres/Frappe) architecture-reviewer — the COMPATIBLE / MINOR / ADR verdict model test-runner — runs your test command task-manager — decomposition is universal skills/ — written for your stack (e.g. fastapi-*, pytest) instead of frappe-* retrospective — the learning loop itself .claude/memory/ — your project's lessons, seeded from your history The two-tool rule + file-handoff discipline CLAUDE.md — your conventions

The roles are the reusable asset. Their bodies are stack-specific and the bootstrap writes them fresh.

docs.title: Worked example — a FastAPI microservice
docs.text:
You're building tap-notifications, a FastAPI service. After the four prompts:

  • CLAUDE.md records: Python 3.12, FastAPI, uv/pip, tests = pytest, lint = ruff, the repo layout.
  • skills/ holds something like fastapi-endpoints, pydantic-models, pytest-fixtures, sqlalchemy-migrations — not frappe-*.
  • feature-builder writes endpoints + Pydantic models + pytest tests in the same commit (the "tests in the same commit" rule carries over; the framework doesn't).
  • code-reviewer checks for FastAPI footguns (sync work in async handlers, unvalidated input) instead of Postgres-vs-MariaDB.
  • test-runner runs pytest -q.
  • prd-author, change-requirement, architecture-reviewer, task-manager, retrospective are essentially the TAP versions with the Frappe references swapped out.

The daily loop is identical to TAP's — only the skills and the three build-loop agents differ.

docs.title: A note on memory tiers (MVP)
docs.text: The bootstrap prompts offer a two-tier memory (lessons.md for load-bearing rules + observations.md for high-churn field notes). TAP LMS deliberately started single-tier (lessons.md only) per its MVP discipline and deferred the second tier until volume justified it. Start single-tier. Add observations.md only when lessons.md is genuinely too noisy to scan. Build the minimum; let evidence pull you to more.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Prompt 0 ran read-only and you answered the three decisions.
  • [ ] Prompt 1 created CLAUDE.md, WORKFLOW.md, .claude/agents/ (each with an INVARIANTS fence), .claude/memory/.
  • [ ] Prompt 2 added retrospective in proposal-only mode.
  • [ ] Prompt 3's seeded lessons were reviewed and the dry-run looked sane.
  • [ ] The verify step confirms: build command works, test command runs, all agent files + memory files exist.
  • [ ] You can drive it: "Write a PRD for X", "Implement CR-NNN", "review the last commits", "run retrospective".

Then open the matching playbook — product or engineering — and start shipping.

docs.title: Adopt it for a new Frappe app
docs.text: Most TAP projects are Frappe (v15 on PostgreSQL). When your new project is also Frappe, you don't start the agent layer from a blank slate — you reuse the Frappe layer that already exists here. This is the Frappe-specific companion to Adopt it for a new project.

docs.title: What's reusable across any Frappe project
docs.text:
Three things lift straight over — they're about Frappe, not about TAP's domain:

  1. The eight frappe-* skills (reference) — DocType, controller, client-script, hooks, api, postgres, test, bench. Copy skills/frappe-* into your new repo unchanged.
  2. The generic Frappe/Postgres rules baked into feature-builder, code-reviewer, test-runner — no ROW_COUNT(), the multi-value filter form, idempotent migrations, _()/__() translations, tests-in-the-same-commit, and the DocType-JSON-and-code-in-one-commit rule.
  3. Everything from the generic methodology — the two-tool model, doc-driven handoffs, the memory + retrospective loop.

docs.title: What you DON'T bring over
docs.text:
TAP-domain rules are about this product, not Frappe — leave them behind:

  • Glific contact-field bundles, the SP state machine (T0–T25), Vocallabs parent calls.
  • The TAP-specific lessons in .claude/memory/lessons.md (the L-0xx rules about Glific / SP / Vocallabs).
  • app/, docs/architecture.md, TAP CRs / ADRs / PRDs.

The line: a rule about how Frappe or Postgres behaves → keep it. A rule about how TAP's program works → drop it.

docs.title: How to set it up
docs.text:
You still run the four bootstrap prompts (cowork-bootstrap.md), but you seed them with the Frappe layer so the generated agents are Frappe-aware from line one:

  1. Copy the skills in first: bash mkdir -p skills cp -r <claude-cowork-code>/skills/frappe-* skills/
  2. Run Prompt 0 (discovery). It detects Frappe (the apps/<name> layout, bench) and flags that Frappe runs from a separate bench location — so you'll symlink your app into the project folder, the same as TAP's app/.
  3. Run Prompt 1 (scaffold), telling it the frappe-* skills are already in skills/. The generated feature-builder / code-reviewer / test-runner will reference them and bake in the Postgres rules.
  4. Prompts 2–3 (retrospective + seed/verify) as normal — but seed lessons from your git history. Start with an empty Frappe-on-Postgres lesson set, not TAP's.

docs.title: Frappe-on-Postgres gotcha
docs.text: If your new app uses PostgreSQL (like TAP), the Postgres skill is the most important file you copy — most Frappe docs assume MariaDB, and the differences (quoting, ROW_COUNT(), JSON casts, migration patch SQL) cause silent bugs. If it uses MariaDB instead, drop frappe-postgres and let Prompt 0 note the difference.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] skills/frappe-* copied into the new repo.
  • [ ] Prompt 0 detected Frappe + flagged the bench symlink.
  • [ ] Generated build agents reference the frappe skills + the Postgres rules.
  • [ ] Memory seeded from your history — no TAP-domain lessons carried over.
  • [ ] The bench symlink is wired (your app ↔ project folder), per SETUP.md.

Then drive it with the engineering playbook.

docs.title: Engineering playbook — CR → build → release
docs.text: For engineers. You live in Claude Code (the build half). You build from named documents, not from chat — a tasks file, a CR, or a BR. This page walks the loop from "there's a spec" to "it's released."

docs.title: What you build from
docs.text:
Inbound Source of truth Start with New feature (from a PRD) docs/.../*-tasks.md (task-manager's output) "Implement TASK-NNN" Behavior change docs/change-requests/CR-NNN-*.md "Implement CR-NNN" Non-trivial bug docs/bug-reports/BR-NNN-*.md (+ tasks) "Implement the BR-NNN fix" Refactor / one-shot tech work a direct task just describe it

The CR gate: if a CR is still Status: Proposed, feature-builder will stop and ask. Never build against a draft — wait for the approver to flip it to Approved (after which the body is immutable).

docs.title: 1. Write the change request (for behavior changes)
docs.text:
If you're changing how an existing feature works, the change starts as a CR, not code:

"Write a CR for: drop students at end of grace instead of pausing."

change-requirement interviews you and writes CR-NNN with the required sections: Motivation, Current Behavior, Proposed Behavior, Scope, Migration, Edge Cases, Acceptance Criteria, Test Plan, Rollback. If it touches schema or system topology, it pulls in architecture-reviewer. The approver flips it to Approved — now it's the build's source of truth.

docs.title: 2. Build it
docs.text:
"Implement CR-NNN" (or "Implement TASK-NNN")

feature-builder reads memory + the CR/PRD + the relevant skills, then builds top-down (data model → logic → API → tests). Two rules it won't break:

  • Tests ship in the same commit as any function with a side effect. No "I'll add tests later."
  • ADR gate: if the work surfaces an un-made architecture decision (new external service, new scheduling cadence, new perf constraint), it stops and spawns architecture-reviewer before continuing.

It ends with a handoff: files changed, acceptance-criteria status, the exact commands to run, and a deploy checklist generated from what the diff touched.

docs.title: 3. Review + test (runs for you)
docs.text:
After a build, the policy is to spawn code-reviewer and test-runner in parallel automatically (trivial edits skip them, and Claude says so). You can also call them by hand:

"Review the diff" · "Run tests"

code-reviewer checks correctness, security, idioms, and that every acceptance criterion has a covering test. test-runner runs the suite and files a task per failure. Recurring findings escalate to the retrospective agent, which turns them into rules so the same mistake doesn't return.

Don't release until review is clean and tests are green.

docs.title: 4. Release
docs.text:
The build loop is automated; release is deliberately manual — a human runs the deploy. The steady-state loop for most services:

review clean + tests green
      ↓
merge / push to the deploy branch
      ↓
run migrations (if any)
      ↓
deploy / restart the service
      ↓
smoke-test the change in the running env
      ↓
watch logs / errors for a short window

Generic release checklist:

  • [ ] Review clean, tests green on the target branch.
  • [ ] Migrations are idempotent and run cleanly on a fresh DB.
  • [ ] Config / secrets / feature flags the change needs are in place.
  • [ ] A rollback path exists (previous build + DB backup) and you know the trigger.
  • [ ] Post-deploy smoke test passes against the running env.
  • [ ] Error/queue volume watched for a window after cutover.

docs.title: TAP LMS release specifics
docs.text:
TAP LMS adds two wrinkles — read these before deploying TAP:

  • Two-folder sync (L-024): you edit app/ in this folder; the bench at ~/frappe-bench/apps/tap_lms is what Frappe runs. Flow: edit here → copy to bench → commit + push from bench → pull back so this folder stays current. Never re-copy files into the bench after the bench has pulled them from git — that creates the untracked-file condition that blocks git pull.
  • The deployment runbook: the full, hard-won procedure (pre-flight probes, bench migrate, bench restart, smoke tests, rollback tree) is docs/deployment-runbook.md. Note it's written for the first-time install; a routine incremental release follows the shorter loop above (copy → commit/push → bench migrate → bench restart → smoke test), using the runbook's smoke-test and rollback sections.
  • migrate vs restart: bench migrate syncs schema + scheduler jobs; bench restart reloads code. Some changes need both — the build handoff's deploy checklist tells you which.

docs.title: 5. Publish the docs (if changed)
docs.text: If the change updates published docs, see Publishing.

docs.title: 6. Close the loop
docs.text:
After a meaningful chunk of work — especially if review caught something — run:

"Run retrospective"

It reads recent reviews, test failures, and git history, and proposes (or, in closed-loop mode, applies) edits to skills/agents/memory so the next build is more correct. This is the part that compounds.

docs.title: Your phrasebook
docs.text:
• "Write a CR for …" — scope a behavior change → change-requirement
  • "Implement CR-NNN" / "Implement TASK-NNN" — build it → feature-builder
  • "Review the diff" / "Review the last N commits" → code-reviewer
  • "Run tests" / "did I break anything" → test-runner
  • "Does our architecture support …" → architecture-reviewer
  • "Run retrospective" — learn from the work → retrospective

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
CR-012: certificate is re-issued every time the completion endpoint is hit (should be once).

  1. "Implement CR-012." feature-builder reads the CR, restates scope, lists files, adds an idempotency guard + a test asserting a second call doesn't re-issue — same commit.
  2. code-reviewer + test-runner run: review clean, tests green.
  3. Release: copy to bench, commit/push, bench migrate (no schema change here, so really just bench restart), smoke-test the endpoint twice, confirm one certificate.
  4. "Run retrospective" — if the bug class (missing idempotency) has recurred, it becomes a rule.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Goal: get both tools pointed at one project folder and confirm the agent layer is wired. ~15 minutes.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Claude account with Claude Code and Cowork access.
  • git, and clone/read access to the project repo (for TAP work, claude-cowork-code).
  • Node.js (for the Claude Code CLI install method below).
  • For TAP LMS specifically: a working Frappe bench on your machine — see SETUP.md. Not needed if you're only planning, or starting a non-Frappe project.

docs.title: 1. Get the project folder
docs.text:
git clone <your-project-repo>
cd <your-project>

Everything — code, docs, the .claude/ agent layer — lives under this one folder. Both tools open it.

docs.title: 2. Install Claude Code (the build half)
docs.text:
Claude Code is the CLI with a terminal. The common install:

npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
claude            # run inside the project folder; sign in when prompted

(See the official Claude Code docs for the latest install options, including the native installer and IDE extensions.) On first run in the folder, Claude Code auto-loads CLAUDE.md as context.

docs.title: 3. Open the same folder in Cowork (the plan half)
docs.text:
Cowork is the planning half. Open the same project folder there. Cowork can read and edit files (specs, PRDs, CRs, reviews) but has no terminal and cannot write .claude/. That split is intentional — it's what keeps planning and building from colliding.

Most projects need no "linking" — both tools just open the same folder. The one exception is a framework that runs code from a separate location (e.g. Frappe's bench): there you symlink that location into the folder. The bootstrap discovery prompt (next page) detects this for you.

docs.title: 4. The one rule to internalise
docs.text: Two tools, one folder — never write the same file at the same time. Plan in Cowork → build in Claude Code → review in Cowork. Sequential. Handoffs travel through named files (a PRD, a CR in docs/), never through chat memory. Full reasoning in Methodology.

docs.title: 5. Verify the wiring
docs.text:
In Claude Code, ask:

"List the agents and skills in this project, and tell me when each one fires."

For a TAP LMS checkout it should name eight agents (prd-author, change-requirement, architecture-reviewer, task-manager, feature-builder, code-reviewer, test-runner, retrospective) and eight frappe-* skills. If it can, the layer is loaded correctly.

Then a read-only smoke check:

"Read CLAUDE.md and WORKFLOW.md and summarise the path for a new feature vs. a behavior change."

If the summary matches WORKFLOW.md, you're set.

docs.title: 6. (TAP LMS only) wire the bench
docs.text: TAP LMS runs from a Frappe bench, so app/ is a symlink into ~/frappe-bench/apps/tap_lms. Bench commands run from ~/frappe-bench. Full steps and the two-folder sync rules: SETUP.md.

docs.title: Where to next
docs.text:
• Starting a brand-new repo/microservice → Adopt it for a new project.
  • In product → Product playbook.
  • In engineering → Engineering playbook.
  • Want the mental model first → Methodology.

docs.title: Methodology — why it's built this way
docs.text: The agents and skills change per project. These principles don't. Understanding them is what lets you drive the system instead of just typing at it.

docs.title: The problem this solves
docs.text: An LLM building software on its own tends to: lose context between sessions, repeat mistakes it already made, and blur planning into building until nobody can tell what was decided versus improvised. This system is six principles that fight each of those.

docs.title: 1. Two tools, one folder
docs.text:
Cowork plans. Claude Code builds. They share one folder and never write the same file at the same time.

Planning (specs, CRs, reviews) and building (code, tests) are different modes of thought, and interleaving them is how half-built ideas get shipped. Splitting them across two tools — one without a terminal — makes the boundary physical. Work flows plan → build → review, sequentially.

docs.title: 2. Documents are the interface
docs.text:
Handoffs travel through named files in docs/, never through chat memory:

  • PRD — the what & why of a new feature.
  • BR — a bug report for a non-trivial defect.
  • CR — a scoped change to existing behavior. Immutable once approved — append-only after.
  • ADR — an architecture decision, with its trade-offs, recorded forever.

A document is reviewable, diffable, and survives the session. Chat doesn't. "Implement CR-012" works tomorrow, on another machine, for another person — because CR-012 is a file. This is also what lets the Cowork↔Code boundary exist at all: the tools don't share memory, but they share the folder.

docs.title: 3. One agent per step
docs.text:
Eight narrow roles instead of one do-everything agent. Each does a single job well and hands off:

prd-author → (architecture-reviewer?) → task-manager → feature-builder → code-reviewer + test-runner
change-requirement → (architecture-reviewer?) → feature-builder → code-reviewer + test-runner
                                                                          ↓ (recurring issue)
                                                                    retrospective

Narrow agents are easier to trust, easier to review, and easier to regenerate for a new stack. A wide agent hides its reasoning; a narrow one's output is a checkable artifact.

docs.title: 4. INVARIANTS — constraints that can't be self-edited
docs.text:
Every agent file has a fenced ## INVARIANTS (do not edit) block listing its core job and the rules it must never weaken — even when the system is editing itself. The retrospective agent (principle 5) can rewrite skills and agents, but it is forbidden from touching anything inside an INVARIANTS fence, including its own. To change an invariant, it files a task for a human.

This is the safety rail that makes self-improvement safe: the system can get smarter without being able to remove its own guardrails.

docs.title: 5. Memory that compounds
docs.text:
The system remembers, in .claude/memory/:

  • lessons.md — load-bearing rules. Append-and-supersede only: a rule is never reworded or deleted; a wrong one is marked superseded with a pointer (ADR-style), so the history of why survives.
  • patterns.md — canonical code idioms to reuse instead of reinventing.
  • Append logs — code-review findings, test failures, decisions.

The retrospective agent reads all of it plus recent git history, finds patterns (a mistake that recurs ≥3 times, or one high-consequence bug), and turns each into a one-line rule that prevents the next occurrence. It audits its own past edits, too — a rule that didn't actually reduce the problem it targeted gets flagged.

Two safety dials:

  • Autonomy — start proposal-only (it suggests; you apply). Graduate to closed-loop (it auto-applies, git is the rollback) once proposals are consistently good.
  • Circuit breaker — lanes (skills, agents, memory) that can be paused. A closed lane blocks writes there until a human reopens it.

This is the compounding part: each recurring mistake becomes a rule, so the project gets more correct over time instead of drifting.

→ Full mechanics: How the system improves itself — the feedback loop, the two triggers, the run sequence, what it may/never touch, and the safety model.

docs.title: 6. Build the minimum, prove it, then expand
docs.text: Tooling follows the same MVP discipline as features: build only what the current work needs; expand because a measurement failed or a real need showed up, never because building has momentum. TAP LMS started single-tier memory and deferred a second tier, deferred a weekly cron, and kept deployment manual — each revisited only when evidence demanded. Apply the same restraint to your own layer: don't add an agent, a memory tier, or a skill until the work asks for it.

docs.title: The payoff
docs.text:
Plan and build stop colliding (1, 2). Decisions become durable and reviewable (2). Each step is a checkable artifact (3). The system can improve itself without removing its guardrails (4, 5). And it stays small until evidence says otherwise (6).

The result: a build loop that closes itself — write the spec, build it, review and test it, learn from it — and gets more correct the longer you run it.

→ Now apply it: Product playbook · Engineering playbook · Adopt it for a new project

docs.title: Product playbook — idea → BR / PRD
docs.text: For product folks. You mostly live in Cowork (the planning half). Your job is to turn ideas and problems into the named documents engineering builds from. You don't need to touch code.

docs.title: Pick the right document
docs.text:
Three situations, three entry agents. Getting this right saves a rewrite:

You have… Entry agent Output Say A new capability ("students should get a certificate") prd-author docs/prds/PRD-NNN-*.md "Write a PRD for …" A non-trivial bug ("re-engagement fires after opt-out") prd-author (bug mode) docs/bug-reports/BR-NNN-*.md "Write a bug report for …" A change to how an existing feature works ("drop students at end of grace instead of pausing") change-requirement docs/change-requests/CR-NNN-*.md "Write a CR for …"

Rule of thumb: new thing → PRD. Broken thing → BR. Different thing → CR. prd-author auto-picks PRD vs. BR by scope; you don't have to.

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
(optional) brainstorm in Cowork
      ↓
"Write a PRD for X"   →  prd-author asks you clarifying questions
      ↓
PRD-NNN lands in docs/prds/   ←  you read it, correct it, approve it
      ↓
"Decompose this into tasks"   →  task-manager → docs/.../*-tasks.md
      ↓
(handoff to engineering — see the Engineering playbook)

docs.title: 1. Brainstorm first (optional but recommended)
docs.text:
Before committing to a doc, think out loud with Claude in Cowork — pressure-test the problem, who it's for, what success looks like, what you're not doing. Cowork ships product brainstorming skills you can lean on. A good brainstorm gives prd-author sharper raw material and means fewer clarifying rounds.

You don't have to brainstorm — if the idea is clear, go straight to "Write a PRD for …".

docs.title: 2. Let prd-author interview you
docs.text: prd-author will probe: the problem, the user, the goal, scope (and non-goals), success metrics, acceptance criteria. Answer plainly. It will also flag if your idea actually raises an architecture question and pull in architecture-reviewer — that's a feature, not a delay; it means a real decision gets recorded as an ADR before code is written.

docs.title: 3. What a good PRD/BR looks like
docs.text:
You're the approver, so know the bar:

  • Problem & why now — the pain, not the solution.
  • User & goal — who, and what they can do after.
  • Scope and non-goals — non-goals are the most valuable lines in the doc; they prevent scope creep.
  • Success metrics — how you'll know it worked.
  • Acceptance criteria — concrete, testable statements. Engineering turns each into a test.
  • (BR) Repro steps + expected vs. actual.

If a section is hand-wavy, send it back before approving. A vague PRD becomes a vague feature.

docs.title: 4. Approve, then hand off
docs.text:
When the PRD reads right, say "Decompose this into tasks" — task-manager breaks it into a backlog and writes a tasks file. That file is the handoff to engineering. (Task lists don't cross the Cowork↔Code boundary; the file does.)

For a behavior change, the gate is different: you flip the CR's Status: Proposed → Approved. After approval the CR body is immutable — further changes are append-only. That immutability is what lets feature-builder trust it as the source of truth.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Idea: "Students should get a certificate when they finish a program."

  1. (Cowork) Brainstorm: who downloads it, what's on it, what about partial completion? Decide certificates are completion-only (non-goal: partial/streak certs, v1).
  2. (Cowork) "Write a PRD for certificate-on-completion." prd-author asks: trigger condition? format (PDF/image)? who can re-download? You answer.
  3. PRD-007 lands in docs/prds/. You read it — the non-goals capture the v1 boundary. You approve.
  4. "Decompose this into tasks." task-manager writes the tasks file: certificate DocType, generation on completion, download endpoint, tests.
  5. Engineering picks it up → Engineering playbook.

docs.title: Your phrasebook
docs.text:
• "Brainstorm a feature for …" — think it through first
  • "Write a PRD for …" — new capability → prd-author
  • "Write a bug report for …" — non-trivial bug → prd-author (BR mode)
  • "Write a CR for …" — change an existing behavior → change-requirement
  • "Does our architecture support …" — sanity-check feasibility → architecture-reviewer
  • "Decompose this into tasks" — ready to hand off → task-manager

docs.title: Publishing the guide
docs.text: How this handbook gets to a public GitHub Pages site while the source repo stays private.

docs.title: The model: private source, public render
docs.text:
claude-cowork-code is a private repo. GitHub Pages can't serve a private site on the current plan, so we don't try. Instead — exactly as the tap-lms-docs site already works — we render the Markdown and push only the built HTML to a separate public repo, whose Pages serves it.

guide/  (private repo)  --mkdocs build-->  HTML  --gh-deploy-->  public docs repo (gh-pages)  -->  Pages URL

Your private source, history, and the rest of the repo never leave the private repo. Only the rendered guide is public.

docs.title: What goes public
docs.text:
This is a separate site from the TAP-LMS product docs (mkdocs.yml → published/). The guide site is configured by mkdocs-guide.yml with docs_dir: guide — so only files under guide/ are published. Nothing else in the repo is rendered.

Keep guide/ generic. It's the public face: no credentials, no internal hostnames, no TAP-LMS internals beyond what's already labelled as examples. The docs_dir: guide boundary is your allowlist — anything you don't want public simply doesn't go in guide/.

docs.title: First-time setup (once)
docs.text:
1. Create a public docs repo. Either in the org (e.g. theapprenticeproject/claude-cowork-code-guide) or a public personal repo. This repo holds only the rendered output.

  2. Add it as a git remote named guide-site: bash git remote add guide-site https://github.com/<owner>/<public-docs-repo>.git

  3. Ensure the docs venv exists (shared with the tap-lms-docs site): bash python3 -m venv .docs-venv .docs-venv/bin/pip install mkdocs-material

  4. Publish: bash ./scripts/publish-guide.sh It builds guide/ with --strict, shows you the target remote, asks for confirmation (the push is public and hard to undo), then gh-deploys to the gh-pages branch of guide-site.

  5. Enable Pages on the public repo: Settings → Pages → Source = gh-pages branch. The URL appears there (e.g. https://<owner>.github.io/<public-docs-repo>/).

  6. Record the URL in README.md and guide/index.md where they say "set after first deploy".

docs.title: Routine publish
docs.text:
After the one-time setup, every update is one command:

./scripts/publish-guide.sh

The gh CLI must be authed as an account with push access to the public repo (here, nithun). Run gh auth status to check.

docs.title: Adding or changing pages
docs.text:
• Drop a new .md into guide/ — it appears in the menu automatically (the config has no nav: block; the menu is built from the files). Add a curated nav: to mkdocs-guide.yml later if you want titles/ordering.
  • Cross-link with relative .md paths ([Methodology](methodology.md)) — mkdocs rewrites them to the right URLs. The same links also work when browsing guide/ directly on GitHub.
  • Re-run ./scripts/publish-guide.sh to push the update.

docs.title: Why two sites, not one
docs.text: The TAP-LMS product docs and this methodology guide have different audiences and different public-vs-internal boundaries. Keeping them as two mkdocs configs (mkdocs.yml and mkdocs-guide.yml) with two site_dirs (site/ and site-guide/) means publishing one never touches the other.

docs.title: How the system improves itself
docs.text: This is what makes the methodology more than "agents that write code." The build loop feeds a learning loop: every review finding and test failure becomes data, and a dedicated agent turns the recurring ones into rules — so the same mistake doesn't happen twice. Over time the project gets more correct on its own.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
feature-builder ──ships──▶ code-reviewer / test-runner
                                  │  write findings + failures
                                  ▼
                     .claude/memory/*.jsonl   (append logs)
                                  │  read every run
                                  ▼
                          retrospective agent
                                  │  recurring pattern → one-line rule
                                  ▼
                  edits skills / agents / lessons.md
                                  │
                                  ▼
                       next build avoids the mistake

The reviewers and testers don't only report to you — they log to files the retrospective reads. That file trail is what closes the loop; nothing depends on a human couriering findings around.

docs.title: When it runs — two triggers
docs.text:
• Manual — you say "run retrospective". A good weekly habit, or after a rough patch.
  • Event-driven — when code-reviewer or test-runner sees the same pattern cross a threshold (≥3 occurrences), it escalates to the retrospective automatically.

(You can also schedule it, but manual + event-driven is plenty to start.)

docs.title: What one run does
docs.text:
1. Check permissions — read circuit-breaker.json: am I allowed to write right now?
  2. Read the evidence — lessons.md, patterns.md, the append logs (code-review-findings.jsonl, test-failures.jsonl, decisions.jsonl), its own past-edit log, and recent CRs / reviews.
  3. Audit itself — for each past edit, did the targeted problem actually stop? Mark it effective / neutral / ineffective.
  4. Extract patterns — promote only what clears the bar (below).
  5. Apply or propose — edit the target file (or write a proposal), one atomic commit each: retro: <what> — <why>.
  6. Log the action so the next run can audit it.

docs.title: What counts as a rule worth adding
docs.text:
All four, or it's skipped:

  1. Recurs ≥3 times, or once with high consequence.
  2. Reduces to a one-line mechanical rule — "when you see X, do Y", not "be careful about X".
  3. Has a clear target file — which skill or agent should hold it.
  4. Isn't already captured (dedupe).

docs.title: What it can and can't touch
docs.text: Edits — to get smarter Never touches — human authority skills/* — rules, examples, anti-patterns app/ source code .claude/agents/* — e.g. add a check to code-reviewer architecture.md, ADRs lessons.md — append-and-supersede, stable IDs CRs, PRDs, bug reports, code-review reports CLAUDE.md — the "lessons" section only the procedural / convention sections of CLAUDE.md

docs.title: Why self-editing is safe
docs.text:
• INVARIANTS fences. Every agent has a ## INVARIANTS (do not edit) block. The retrospective can rewrite agents and skills but is forbidden from touching anything inside a fence — even its own. If it thinks an invariant is wrong, it files a task for a human. It cannot remove its own guardrails.
  • Autonomy dial. Start proposal-only (it writes suggestions to docs/retrospective-runs/; you apply the good ones). Graduate to closed-loop once proposals are consistently good — then it applies directly and git is the rollback.
  • Circuit breaker. Three lanes — skills, agents, memory. A closed lane blocks all writes there until you reopen it. And the self-audit closes a lane automatically if the same edit keeps getting reverted.
  • Atomic + reversible. One edit per commit, clearly messaged, on a git-tracked tree. A bad edit is one git revert away — and the next run notices the revert and learns from it.

docs.title: How you drive it
docs.text:
• Run it: "run retrospective" (or "scan for patterns").
  • Proposal-only mode: review docs/retrospective-runs/proposal-*.md and apply what you agree with.
  • Closed-loop mode: skim the retro: commits in git log; revert anything you disagree with — the system treats your revert as a signal and adjusts.

The compounding effect is the whole point: a one-time bug becomes a permanent rule, so the curve bends toward fewer repeated mistakes the longer the project runs.

→ Back to the methodology · drive it from the engineering playbook.

docs.title: Frappe reference skills
docs.text:
Most TAP work is Frappe (v15, PostgreSQL — not MariaDB). These eight skill files are the team's accumulated Frappe/Postgres knowledge — the patterns and the landmines — that the build agents read before writing code. They're drop-in reusable: copy skills/frappe-* into any new Frappe project and its feature-builder / code-reviewer / test-runner inherit the same hard-won rules.

These are generic Frappe knowledge, not TAP-domain logic. TAP-specific rules (Glific, the SP state machine, Vocallabs) live in .claude/memory/ lessons, not here.

docs.title: The skills
docs.text:
Read the one that matches what you're about to do:

Skill Read before… DocType creating/altering a DocType — fields, naming, child tables, permissions Controller validation, lifecycle hooks, controller methods Client script form / client-side behavior Hooks cross-DocType events, cron, fixtures API REST, whitelisted methods, webhooks, integrations Postgres raw SQL, indexes, migrations — the Postgres-vs-MariaDB landmines Test tests, fixtures, factories, coverage Bench bench commands, console, sites, the diagnostic toolkit

docs.title: Why Postgres matters most
docs.text: TAP runs Frappe on PostgreSQL, while most Frappe documentation assumes MariaDB. The Postgres skill is the highest-leverage of the eight — ROW_COUNT(), backtick quoting, JSON::text casts, creation timezone, and multi-value filter forms all differ. Any new Frappe-on-Postgres project should read it first.

docs.title: Reusing these on a new Frappe project
docs.text: See Adopt it for a new Frappe app — copy these skills in as-is, keep the generic Frappe rules in the build agents, drop the TAP-domain lessons.

docs.title: Frappe API skill
docs.text:
STOP — read this first if the endpoint is consumed by Glific: docs/api-standard-glific.md is the binding contract for every @frappe.whitelist() endpoint that Glific calls. It overrides Frappe defaults: NO message wrapper (use frappe.local.response.update()), flat scalars only, no arrays, success + status envelope, HTTP 200 even for business errors, snake_case ASCII keys. Read it end-to-end before writing or modifying the endpoint, and run the curl-test (Rule 10) before declaring done.

Frappe ships three API surfaces:

  1. Whitelisted methods — RPC-style. You decorate a Python function and it's reachable as /api/method/<dotted.path>. This is the workhorse.
  2. REST resource API — auto-generated CRUD over DocTypes at /api/resource/<DocType>. Good for generic admin tools and simple integrations.
  3. Web view / portal pages — @frappe.whitelist(allow_guest=True) plus a Jinja template, for public-facing endpoints.

Pick #1 for almost everything custom; #2 only when you genuinely want generic CRUD; #3 for anonymous reads.

docs.title: Whitelisted methods
docs.text:
# app/tap_lms/api.py
import frappe
from frappe import _


@frappe.whitelist()
def enroll(student: str, course: str) -> dict:
    """Enroll a student in a course. Idempotent."""
    if not frappe.db.exists("Student", student):
        frappe.throw(_("Student {0} not found").format(student))
    if not frappe.db.exists("Course", course):
        frappe.throw(_("Course {0} not found").format(course))

    existing = frappe.db.get_value(
        "Course Enrollment",
        {"student": student, "course": course, "status": "Active"},
        "name",
    )
    if existing:
        return {"enrollment": existing, "created": False}

    doc = frappe.get_doc({
        "doctype": "Course Enrollment",
        "student": student,
        "course": course,
        "status": "Active",
    }).insert()
    return {"enrollment": doc.name, "created": True}

Reachable at:

POST /api/method/tap_lms.api.enroll
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
student=STU-001&course=CS101

Returned JSON wraps the value in {"message": ...}. Clients should read response.message.

docs.title: allow_guest
docs.text:
@frappe.whitelist(allow_guest=True)
def public_course_list():
    return frappe.get_all("Course", filters={"is_published": 1}, fields=["name", "title"])

Without allow_guest=True, the method requires an authenticated session. Be deliberate; guest endpoints are the most common security hole.

docs.title: methods=
docs.text:
@frappe.whitelist(methods=["POST"])
def submit_attempt(...): ...

Restrict HTTP verbs. Defaults to GET+POST. Use methods=["POST"] for state-changing endpoints so a CSRF-style accidental GET can't trigger a write.

docs.title: Type hints and validation
docs.text:
Frappe doesn't currently coerce types from query strings — everything arrives as strings. Either coerce manually:

@frappe.whitelist()
def list_attempts(course: str, limit: int = 20) -> list:
    limit = int(limit)
    ...

Or wrap with pydantic / attrs if your app already uses them.

docs.title: REST resource API
docs.text:
Out of the box:

  • GET /api/resource/Course — list (respects user permissions)
  • GET /api/resource/Course/CS101 — single doc
  • POST /api/resource/Course — create (body = JSON dict)
  • PUT /api/resource/Course/CS101 — update
  • DELETE /api/resource/Course/CS101 — delete

Query params: ?fields=["name","title"]&filters=[["is_published","=",1]]&limit_page_length=50&order_by=creation desc.

The resource API runs through the same permission system as the desk. A user/role without read on the DocType gets 403.

docs.title: API Key + Secret (preferred for server-to-server)
docs.text:
User sets up an API Key + API Secret under their User profile. Calling code sends:

Authorization: token <api_key>:<api_secret>

Generate programmatically:

user = frappe.get_doc("User", "integrations@tap.example")
api_secret = frappe.generate_hash(length=15)
user.api_key = frappe.generate_hash(length=15)
user.api_secret = api_secret
user.save(ignore_permissions=True)
# Show api_secret to user once — it's hashed at rest.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0
docs.text: Frappe is itself an OAuth provider — set up an OAuth Client record, then point a third-party client at /api/method/frappe.integrations.oauth2.authorize. Use this when a user is granting a foreign app access on their behalf. Skip for internal services; API keys are simpler.

docs.title: Session cookies
docs.text: For SPAs served from the same origin, the session cookie set by /api/method/login works fine. For cross-origin, you'll need to handle CORS (see cors_domains in common_site_config.json) and CSRF (Frappe sets X-Frappe-CSRF-Token for authenticated sessions; pass it back on writes).

docs.title: Webhooks (incoming)
docs.text:
Treat as untrusted input. Verify signatures:

import hmac, hashlib

@frappe.whitelist(allow_guest=True, methods=["POST"])
def receive_payment_webhook():
    raw = frappe.request.get_data()
    signature = frappe.request.headers.get("X-Webhook-Signature", "")
    expected = hmac.new(
        frappe.conf.payment_webhook_secret.encode(),
        raw,
        hashlib.sha256,
    ).hexdigest()
    if not hmac.compare_digest(signature, expected):
        frappe.throw(_("Bad signature"), exc=frappe.AuthenticationError)

    payload = frappe.parse_json(raw)
    frappe.enqueue(
        "tap_lms.tap_lms.payments.handle_webhook",
        payload=payload,
        queue="short",
    )
    return {"ok": True}

Always offload work to a queue — webhooks demand fast 200 responses.

docs.title: Webhooks (outgoing)
docs.text: Frappe has a built-in Webhook DocType: configure URL + headers + body template + trigger DocType + event. No code needed for most outgoing webhooks.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text: Frappe has a basic per-IP/per-user limiter (enable_rate_limit in site config). For richer needs, put nginx in front and rate-limit there, or wrap the method with a custom decorator that reads/writes a Redis counter via frappe.cache().

docs.title: Error responses
docs.text:
frappe.throw(_("...")) produces a 417 with the message. For RESTful 400/404/403 codes:

import frappe
from werkzeug.exceptions import NotFound, BadRequest

@frappe.whitelist()
def get_course(name):
    if not frappe.db.exists("Course", name):
        raise NotFound(f"Course {name} not found")
    return frappe.get_doc("Course", name).as_dict()

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
Frappe doesn't version /api/method paths. If your API has external consumers, version it yourself by namespace:

/api/method/tap_lms.api.v1.enroll
/api/method/tap_lms.api.v2.enroll

Don't break v1 once published.

docs.title: Public API contract — parameter names matter
docs.text:
On TAP LMS, whitelisted method parameter names are public contract. Glific flows reference them directly (and contact-field names too — lesson L-008). Renaming content_id → assignment_id without an alias silently breaks every Glific flow node that calls the API. This has bitten us twice (CR-2026-05-10 #H2).

Always add a backward-compat alias for at least one release cycle, and log a deprecation warning when the old name is used. Pattern P-006:

@frappe.whitelist()
def save_submission(student_id, assignment_id=None, content_id=None, **kwargs):
    if assignment_id is None and content_id is not None:
        assignment_id = content_id
        frappe.log_error(
            "Deprecated: save_submission called with content_id; "
            "rename to assignment_id",
            "API deprecation",
        )
    if assignment_id is None:
        frappe.throw(_("assignment_id is required"))
    ...

Lesson L-009. Code-reviewer flags every rename without an alias as HIGH severity.

docs.title: External calls must retry — Glific, RabbitMQ, anything off-box
docs.text:
Calls to Glific (update_contact_fields, start_contact_flow) and RabbitMQ publishes from inside whitelisted methods need retry + dead-letter behaviour. The state has already committed in PG by the time the external call runs; a silent failure leaves Glific cache stale or submissions lost (CR-2026-05-10 #H3, #H4).

Use frappe.enqueue with retry=N rather than calling the external service inline:

def _sync_contact_fields(pe):
    try:
        update_contact_fields(pe.glific_id, build_field_dict(pe))
    except Exception as e:
        frappe.log_error(
            f"Glific sync failed for {pe.glific_id}: {e}",
            "Glific sync",
        )
        frappe.enqueue(
            "tap_lms.summer_program.glific_extensions.retry_contact_fields",
            queue="short", retry=3,
            pe_name=pe.name,
        )

Lesson L-015, pattern P-007.

docs.title: Glific contact fields require TWO mutations, not one
docs.text:
updateContact (the mutation we used for years) writes a value into the contact's fields JSON column but does not register the field's DEFINITION. Without a definition row in Glific's contacts_fields table, the field is invisible to the Flow Editor: no dropdown entry, @contact.fields.<shortcode> renders as literal text, and webhook query params can't surface it. Confirmed by Glific support 2026-05-26.

3-step protocol when adding any new contact field:

  1. Add the CF_X = "shortcode" constant in summer_program/constants.py.
  2. Add it to every push payload that should carry the field:
  3. state_machine._enqueue_contact_field_sync (recurring per-transition sync)
  4. program_enrollment_api._process_pe_chunk and process_glific_contact (enrollment-time push)
  5. dev_tools.reconcile_pe_to_glific (operator-driven reconcile)
  6. Add (shortcode, "Display Name") to SP_CONTACT_FIELD_DEFINITIONS in dev_tools.py AND re-run dev_tools.bootstrap_sp_contact_fields() on every Glific org (dev, prod). The helper is idempotent — already-registered fields return "shortcode already taken" which we treat as success.

Skipping step 3 means the value lands in the JSON cache (visible in the contact profile) but flow templates render @contact.fields.X as literal text.

Multi-tenant Glific boundary. Several programs share the same Glific organization (TLM, scert, pocflow, plus SP). Legacy keys like streak, gems, bonus_points, current_activity_points are owned by other programs — the SP backend must not write to them. The SP namespace is exactly the 29-30 fields registered by bootstrap_sp_contact_fields(). Writing outside that namespace silently clobbers data other programs depend on. Lesson L-053.

docs.title: Audit-field-as-idempotency-anchor pattern
docs.text:
When the same logical write can be produced by multiple writers (sync API + async worker; in-request handler + scheduled cron), an audit column on the row coordinates them without locking. Pre-fill the field at the upstream-write site; downstream hooks gate on the field to skip:

# In-request handler awards points and pre-fills the audit field
@frappe.whitelist()
def complete_content(student_id, content_id, ...):
    pts = award_points_now(student_id, content_id)
    frappe.enqueue(
        "tap_lms.summer_program.background_jobs.job_log_content_completion",
        queue="short",
        student_id=student_id,
        content_id=content_id,
        points_awarded=pts,   # ← carry the already-awarded amount
        ...
    )

# Worker creates the audit row with points_awarded ALREADY SET
def job_log_content_completion(student_id, content_id, points_awarded=None, ...):
    log = frappe.get_doc({
        "doctype": "StudentContentLog",
        ...,
        "points_awarded": cint(points_awarded) if points_awarded is not None else 0,
    })
    log.insert(ignore_permissions=True)

# after_insert hook reads the gate field and skips if upstream awarded
def handle_content_log(scl, method=None):
    if (scl.points_awarded or 0) > 0:
        return   # already awarded by upstream caller; nothing to do
    award_points(scl)

The pattern is pattern P-010 (proposed; full form expanded from P-005 "idempotency anchor written first"). Used correctly, it eliminates the need for cross-process locks for write-once audit data.

docs.title: Good API hygiene
docs.text:
• Return predictable shapes. Don't return a Document one call and a dict the next.
  • Document each endpoint with a docstring; bench generates docs from them.
  • Use frappe.has_permission(doctype, ptype, doc=name) to check permissions explicitly when bypassing default checks.
  • Log unusual conditions via frappe.log_error(message, title). They land in the Error Log DocType and are filterable.

docs.title: Testing API endpoints
docs.text:
bench --site <site> execute tap_lms.api.enroll --kwargs '{"student": "STU-001", "course": "CS101"}' runs a method with the desired session. Combine with bench console for ad-hoc poking.

For automated tests, see the frappe-test skill — Frappe's test runner sets up an authenticated context so you can call whitelisted methods directly.

docs.title: Frappe bench skill
docs.text:
Launch context: project root. For bench commands, cd ~/frappe-bench first.

bench is a CLI wrapper around Frappe that orchestrates: per-site DBs, app installation, migrations, asset builds, workers, scheduler, and backups. The cardinal rule is: most "did my change take effect?" mysteries are solved by bench restart and bench --site <site> clear-cache.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
A bench is a directory with this structure:

frappe-bench/
├── apps/
│   ├── frappe/
│   ├── erpnext/
│   └── tap_lms/        ← your custom app
├── sites/
│   ├── apps.txt
│   ├── common_site_config.json
│   └── <sitename>/
│       ├── site_config.json
│       ├── public/
│       └── private/
├── env/                # Python virtualenv
└── config/             # nginx, supervisor, redis configs

apps/<app> is a normal git repo — work there exactly like any other Python package.

docs.title: First-time setup (Postgres)
docs.text:
# Install bench CLI
pip install frappe-bench

# Init a bench tracking v15
bench init --frappe-branch version-15 frappe-bench

cd frappe-bench

# Tell bench to use Postgres for new sites
bench set-config -g db_type postgres
bench set-config -g db_host 127.0.0.1
bench set-config -g db_port 5432

# Create a new site backed by Postgres
bench new-site tap.local \
    --db-type postgres \
    --db-host 127.0.0.1 \
    --db-root-username postgres \
    --admin-password admin

# Get your custom app
bench get-app tap_lms <git-url-or-local-path>
bench --site tap.local install-app tap_lms

# Start the dev server (web + scheduler + workers + watcher)
bench start

docs.title: Day-to-day commands
docs.text: Every site-scoped command takes --site <name> (or set a default with bench use <site>).

docs.title: Migration & schema
docs.text:
bench --site tap.local migrate          # Apply DocType JSON changes + run patches
bench --site tap.local reload-doctype "Course Enrollment"  # Re-read one DocType from disk
bench --site tap.local clear-cache      # Wipe metadata + Redis caches
bench --site tap.local clear-website-cache

migrate is the one you'll run constantly. If a migration fails midway, fix the cause and re-run; patches that already ran are skipped (tracked in tabPatch Log).

docs.title: App lifecycle
docs.text:
bench new-app tap_lms                   # Scaffold a new app
bench --site tap.local install-app tap_lms
bench --site tap.local uninstall-app tap_lms
bench --site tap.local list-apps

docs.title: Build & assets
docs.text:
bench build                  # Build all apps' JS/CSS bundles
bench build --app tap_lms    # Just yours
bench watch                  # Live rebuild on change (dev)

After editing .bundle.js files or anything in public/, run bench build (or have bench start running, which calls watch).

docs.title: Restart
docs.text:
bench restart                # Reload web workers + queue workers + scheduler
bench restart --supervisor   # Production: restart via supervisorctl

Restart whenever you change hooks.py, install/uninstall an app, or change Python code that's imported at startup. Lifecycle methods inside DocType controllers don't need a restart (they're imported per request).

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
bench --site tap.local backup                    # SQL only
bench --site tap.local backup --with-files       # SQL + private/public files
bench --site tap.local backup --compress
ls sites/tap.local/private/backups/              # ← they land here

Restore:

bench --site tap.local restore <path/to/backup.sql.gz> \
    --with-public-files <path/to/files.tar> \
    --with-private-files <path/to/private.tar>

For Postgres, the backups are produced by pg_dump; restore uses pg_restore under the hood.

docs.title: Common operational issues
docs.text:
"My JS changes don't show up" — Browser cache, then bench build, then bench --site <site> clear-cache, in that order.

"My new doc_event doesn't fire" — hooks.py change without bench restart. Restart and retry.

"Scheduler isn't running my hourly job" — In dev, bench start must be running. In prod, supervisor must be up and enabled_scheduler_events in site config must include the relevant frequency. Check tabScheduled Job Log for evidence the scheduler is alive.

"I added a new entry to scheduler_events.cron in hooks.py, ran bench restart, and it never fires" — Restart reloads code but does NOT re-sync scheduler_events into the DB. Frappe stores scheduler entries in the tabScheduled Job Type table; that table is populated from hooks.py only by bench --site <site> migrate. Rule: after editing scheduler_events, run bench --site <site> migrate AND bench restart. Editing doc_events only requires restart. Verify by querying tabScheduled Job Type WHERE method LIKE '<your_module>%' after migrate.

"My RQ background job runs but no data appears (silent success)" — The job's outer except swallows exceptions without re-raising. RQ marks the job "finished" because no exception propagated, but the work the job was supposed to do never landed. Rule: every RQ job's outer except branch must end with raise (after any frappe.db.rollback() + frappe.log_error). Check FailedJobRegistry to see if your jobs are actually failing: in bench console, from tap_lms.summer_program.sp_console import queue_failures_for; queue_failures_for("<func_name>").

"Site won't load: connection refused" — Postgres or Redis isn't running. pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5432, redis-cli ping.

"bench migrate fails with permission denied" — The Postgres user lacks CREATE on the DB. Either grant it (GRANT ALL ON DATABASE <db> TO <user>) or run migrate as a privileged user once.

"Out of memory during build" — bench build runs node/esbuild and can be hungry. On small servers, NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=2048 bench build.

docs.title: Production knobs
docs.text:
bench setup production <user> writes nginx + supervisor configs. After:

sudo supervisorctl reread && sudo supervisorctl update
sudo nginx -s reload

bench setup nginx regenerates nginx config (run after adding a site or changing SSL). bench setup supervisor regenerates worker configs (run after changing worker counts in common_site_config.json).

For Postgres specifically, ensure pg_hba.conf allows the bench user from 127.0.0.1 (host <db> <user> 127.0.0.1/32 md5) and max_connections is high enough — calculate (workers × queues) + gunicorn workers + a buffer and add 20%.

docs.title: Console — use sp_console instead of pasted snippets
docs.text:
Bench console is IPython under the hood. Two failure modes hit repeatedly when pasting raw diagnostic snippets:

  1. Generator/closure-scope NameError. A def or genexp inside a multiline cell sometimes fails to capture imports declared in the same cell. Workarounds (split into separate cells; inline everything) are fragile.
  2. Placeholder-syntax SyntaxError. Snippets with placeholders like [...names from above...] parse as invalid Python before any comment is read.

The fix is to call functions, not paste cells. Save the helper code below to a personal file on the bench server (the team convention is ~/sp_console.py), then load it into your console session.

These helpers are developer tooling only — NOT part of the shipped tap_lms app. They live in this skill file as a copy-paste reference (one canonical version everyone shares) rather than in app/tap_lms/ because they don't belong in production code paths.

cohort_status_breakdown("palv2-test-BT52231")     # status × resolved_flow_state counts
collection_diff("palv2-test-BT52231", main_group_id="20529")  # MAIN_ELIGIBLE_STATES-aware
enqueue_health()                                  # Redis + queues + workers + smoke test + recents

scheduled_crons()                                 # verify bench migrate registered new entries

docs.title: When to update this skill file
docs.text:
When you write a new diagnostic during a session, save it BOTH to your local ~/sp_console.py AND propose appending the function to this skill file via PR. The skill file is the canonical version; local files are working copies that should match.

Conventions: - Top-level def (no closures over imports declared in console). - First line is frappe.db.rollback() (clears any poisoned txn from a prior cell). - Accept explicit string args, not in-cell mutable references. - Return a dict; gate the print output on verbose=True. - Read-only by default; prefix mutating functions with repair_.

docs.title: The helper module — copy this entire block to ~/sp_console.py
docs.text:
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
# Developer console toolkit. NOT part of the shipped tap_lms app.
# Canonical version lives in skills/frappe-bench/SKILL.md.
# Save this file at ~/sp_console.py on the bench server; load with
#   exec(open("/home/<user>/sp_console.py").read())
# inside `bench --site <site> console`.

import json
import time
from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional

import frappe
import requests
from frappe.utils import now_datetime


# ── PE / student state inspection ───────────────────────────────

def pe_health(student_id: str, verbose: bool = True) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """3-way comparison: PE row / Glific contact / get_student_state API."""
    frappe.db.rollback()

    pe_row = frappe.db.sql(
        """
        SELECT name, glific_id, program_status, current_week, current_path,
               current_tier, resolved_flow_state, journey_label,
               total_points, current_streak, special_gems,
               total_activity_points, weekly_activity_points,
               total_quiz_points, weekly_quiz_points, bonus_quiz_points,
               total_submission_points, weekly_submission_points,
               weekly_submission_done, weekly_video_done,
               current_escalation_step, current_escalation_type,
               in_grace_window, grace_window_end_at,
               next_action_at, next_action_type
          FROM "tabProgramEnrollment"
         WHERE student = %s AND program_status IN ('active', 'paused')
         ORDER BY modified DESC LIMIT 1
        """,
        (student_id,), as_dict=True,
    )
    if not pe_row:
        if verbose:
            print(f"no active/paused PE for {student_id}")
        return {"pe": None, "glific": None, "api": None, "drift": []}
    pe = pe_row[0]

    glific = _fetch_glific_contact(pe["glific_id"]) if pe.get("glific_id") else {}
    api = _call_get_student_state(student_id)

    drift = []
    pairs = [
        ("resolved_flow_state", "resolved_flow_state"),
        ("current_week", "current_week"),
        ("current_streak", "current_streak"),
        ("special_gems", "special_gems"),
        ("total_points", "total_points"),
        ("total_quiz_points", "total_quiz_points"),
        ("bonus_quiz_points", "bonus_quiz_points"),
        ("weekly_quiz_points", "weekly_quiz_points"),
        ("weekly_activity_points", "weekly_activity_points"),
        ("weekly_submission_points", "weekly_submission_points"),
        ("escalation_type", "current_escalation_type"),
    ]
    for glific_key, pe_key in pairs:
        pe_val = pe.get(pe_key)
        glific_val = glific.get(glific_key)
        if glific_val is None:
            continue
        if str(pe_val) != str(glific_val):
            drift.append({"key": glific_key, "pe": pe_val, "glific": glific_val})

    if verbose:
        print(f"\nPE.{pe['name']}  student={student_id}  status={pe['program_status']}")
        print(f"  state={pe['resolved_flow_state']}  week={pe['current_week']}  "
              f"tier={pe['current_tier']}  path={pe['current_path']}")
        print(f"  total={pe['total_points']}  streak={pe['current_streak']}  "
              f"gems={pe['special_gems']}  bonus={pe['bonus_quiz_points']}")
        print(f"  weekly: video={pe['weekly_video_done']} "
              f"submission={pe['weekly_submission_done']} "
              f"q={pe['weekly_quiz_points']} a={pe['weekly_activity_points']} "
              f"s={pe['weekly_submission_points']}")
        if pe['current_escalation_step']:
            print(f"  escalation step={pe['current_escalation_step']} "
                  f"type={pe['current_escalation_type']}")
        if pe['next_action_type']:
            print(f"  next: {pe['next_action_type']} at {pe['next_action_at']}")
        print(f"\ndrift items ({len(drift)}):")
        for d in drift:
            print(f"  {d['key']:30s} PE={d['pe']!r:15s} Glific={d['glific']!r}")

    return {"pe": pe, "glific": glific, "api": api, "drift": drift}


def pe_events(student_id_or_pe: str, limit: int = 20,
              verbose: bool = True) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """Last N ProgramEventLog rows. FK column is `enrollment` (L-052)."""
    frappe.db.rollback()

    if student_id_or_pe.startswith("ST"):
        pe_name = frappe.db.get_value(
            "ProgramEnrollment",
            {"student": student_id_or_pe,
             "program_status": ["in", ["active", "paused"]]},
            "name", order_by="modified desc",
        )
    else:
        pe_name = student_id_or_pe

    if not pe_name:
        if verbose:
            print(f"no PE found for {student_id_or_pe}")
        return []

    rows = frappe.db.sql(
        """
        SELECT creation, event_type, trigger_source,
               old_value, new_value,
               LEFT(details::text, 200) AS details
          FROM "tabProgramEventLog"
         WHERE enrollment = %s
         ORDER BY creation DESC LIMIT %s
        """,
        (pe_name, limit), as_dict=True,
    )
    if verbose:
        print(f"\nLast {len(rows)} events for PE {pe_name}:")
        for r in rows:
            print(f"  {r['creation']}  {r['event_type']:30s}  "
                  f"src={r['trigger_source']!r:14s}  "
                  f"{r['old_value']!r} → {r['new_value']!r}")
    return rows


# ── Cohort-wide diagnostics ─────────────────────────────────────

def cohort_drift(batch_name: str, verbose: bool = True) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Read-only cohort sweep via dev_tools.reconcile_batch_to_glific(dry_run=True)."""
    frappe.db.rollback()
    from tap_lms.summer_program import dev_tools
    return dev_tools.reconcile_batch_to_glific(
        batch_name, dry_run=True, verbose=verbose,
    )


def cohort_status_breakdown(batch_name: str,
                            verbose: bool = True) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """PE counts grouped by (program_status, resolved_flow_state)."""
    frappe.db.rollback()
    rows = frappe.db.sql(
        """
        SELECT program_status, resolved_flow_state, COUNT(*) AS n
          FROM "tabProgramEnrollment"
         WHERE batch = %s
         GROUP BY program_status, resolved_flow_state
         ORDER BY n DESC
        """,
        (batch_name,), as_dict=True,
    )
    if verbose:
        print(f"\nPE breakdown for {batch_name}:")
        for r in rows:
            print(f"  {r['program_status']:12s} "
                  f"{r['resolved_flow_state'] or '-':30s}  {r['n']}")
    return rows


def collection_diff(batch_name: str, main_group_id: str,
                    verbose: bool = True) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Filter PEs by MAIN_ELIGIBLE_STATES (CR-005) before diffing against
    the Glific group. grace_waiting / escalation / paused are excluded
    by design, not 'missing' (L-055)."""
    frappe.db.rollback()
    from tap_lms.summer_program.collection_membership import MAIN_ELIGIBLE_STATES
    from tap_lms.glific_integration import (
        get_glific_settings, get_glific_auth_headers,
    )

    pes = frappe.db.sql(
        """
        SELECT pe.name, pe.student, pe.glific_id,
               pe.program_status, pe.resolved_flow_state
          FROM "tabProgramEnrollment" pe
         WHERE pe.batch = %s
           AND pe.program_status IN ('active', 'paused')
        """,
        (batch_name,), as_dict=True,
    )
    eligible_by_gid = {}
    for p in pes:
        if p["glific_id"] and p["resolved_flow_state"] in MAIN_ELIGIBLE_STATES:
            eligible_by_gid[str(p["glific_id"])] = p
    eligible_gids = set(eligible_by_gid.keys())

    settings = get_glific_settings()
    r = requests.post(
        f"{settings.api_url}/api",
        json={
            "query": "query g($id: ID!){group(id:$id){group{id contacts{id phone}}}}",
            "variables": {"id": str(main_group_id)},
        },
        headers=get_glific_auth_headers(), timeout=30,
    ).json()
    contacts = (((r.get("data") or {}).get("group") or {}).get("group") or {}).get("contacts") or []
    collection_gids = {str(c.get("id")) for c in contacts}

    missing = eligible_gids - collection_gids
    extra = collection_gids - eligible_gids

    if verbose:
        print(f"\nEligible for main collection: {len(eligible_gids)}")
        print(f"Collection members on Glific:  {len(collection_gids)}")
        print(f"\nMissing from collection ({len(missing)}):")
        for gid in missing:
            p = eligible_by_gid[gid]
            print(f"  {p['name']}  student={p['student']}  gid={gid}  "
                  f"state={p['resolved_flow_state']}")
        print(f"\nExtra in collection ({len(extra)}):")
        for gid in extra:
            print(f"  gid={gid}")

    return {
        "eligible_gids": list(eligible_gids),
        "collection_gids": list(collection_gids),
        "missing": list(missing),
        "extra": list(extra),
    }


# ── Background-job + queue health ───────────────────────────────

def enqueue_health(verbose: bool = True) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """6-step roll-up: Redis ping + queues + workers + recent jobs + smoke test."""
    frappe.db.rollback()
    out: Dict[str, Any] = {}

    try:
        from frappe.utils.background_jobs import get_redis_conn
        out["redis_ping"] = get_redis_conn().ping()
    except Exception as e:
        out["redis_ping"] = f"ERROR: {e}"

    try:
        from frappe.utils.background_jobs import get_queue
        queues_info = {}
        for name in ("short", "default", "long"):
            q = get_queue(name)
            queues_info[name] = {
                "actual_name": q.name,
                "depth": len(q),
                "failed": q.failed_job_registry.count,
                "scheduled": q.scheduled_job_registry.count,
                "started": q.started_job_registry.count,
            }
        out["queues"] = queues_info
    except Exception as e:
        out["queues"] = f"ERROR: {e}"

    try:
        from rq import Worker
        from frappe.utils.background_jobs import get_redis_conn
        workers = Worker.all(connection=get_redis_conn())
        out["workers"] = [
            {"name": w.name, "state": w.get_state(),
             "queues": [qq.name for qq in w.queues],
             "birth": str(w.birth_date)}
            for w in workers
        ]
    except Exception as e:
        out["workers"] = f"ERROR: {e}"

    try:
        from rq.registry import FailedJobRegistry, FinishedJobRegistry
        from rq.job import Job
        from frappe.utils.background_jobs import get_queue
        recents = {}
        for name in ("short", "default", "long"):
            q = get_queue(name)
            fin = FinishedJobRegistry(queue=q)
            fail = FailedJobRegistry(queue=q)
            recents[name] = {"finished": [], "failed": []}
            for jid in fin.get_job_ids(0, 5):
                try:
                    j = Job.fetch(jid, connection=q.connection)
                    recents[name]["finished"].append({
                        "ended_at": str(j.ended_at), "func": j.func_name,
                    })
                except Exception:
                    pass
            for jid in fail.get_job_ids(0, 5):
                try:
                    j = Job.fetch(jid, connection=q.connection)
                    recents[name]["failed"].append({
                        "ended_at": str(j.ended_at), "func": j.func_name,
                        "exc_excerpt": (j.exc_info or "")[:200].replace("\n", " "),
                    })
                except Exception:
                    pass
        out["recent_jobs"] = recents
    except Exception as e:
        out["recent_jobs"] = f"ERROR: {e}"

    try:
        job = frappe.enqueue(
            "frappe.utils.background_jobs.test_job",
            queue="short", timeout=10, s=1,
        )
        deadline = time.time() + 10
        status = job.get_status()
        while time.time() < deadline and status not in ("finished", "failed"):
            time.sleep(0.5)
            status = job.get_status(refresh=True)
        out["smoke_test"] = {
            "final_status": status, "id": job.id,
            "exc_excerpt": (job.exc_info or "")[:300] if status == "failed" else None,
        }
    except Exception as e:
        out["smoke_test"] = {"error": str(e)}

    if verbose:
        print("== Redis ===========================================")
        print(f"  ping = {out['redis_ping']}")
        print("\n== Queues ==========================================")
        if isinstance(out["queues"], dict):
            for name, info in out["queues"].items():
                tag = "✓" if info["depth"] < 100 and info["failed"] == 0 else "⚠"
                print(f"  {tag} {name:8s}  depth={info['depth']:4d}  "
                      f"started={info['started']:3d}  "
                      f"failed={info['failed']:3d}  "
                      f"scheduled={info['scheduled']:3d}")
        else:
            print(f"  {out['queues']}")
        print("\n== Workers =========================================")
        if isinstance(out["workers"], list):
            print(f"  {len(out['workers'])} workers registered")
            for w in out["workers"]:
                print(f"    {w['name']}  state={w['state']}  queues={w['queues']}")
        else:
            print(f"  {out['workers']}")
        print("\n== Smoke test ======================================")
        if isinstance(out["smoke_test"], dict):
            st = out["smoke_test"].get("final_status")
            mark = "✓" if st == "finished" else "✗"
            print(f"  {mark} test_job final_status = {st}")
            if st == "failed":
                print(f"    {out['smoke_test'].get('exc_excerpt')}")
        else:
            print(f"  {out['smoke_test']}")
        print("\n== Recent jobs =====================================")
        if isinstance(out["recent_jobs"], dict):
            for name, info in out["recent_jobs"].items():
                print(f"  {name}: {len(info['finished'])} finished, "
                      f"{len(info['failed'])} failed (last 5)")
                for f in info["failed"]:
                    print(f"    FAILED {f['ended_at']}  {f['func']}: {f['exc_excerpt']}")

    return out


def queue_failures_for(func_name_pattern: str, limit: int = 20,
                       verbose: bool = True) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """Search RQ FailedJobRegistry for a function-name substring.
    Use BEFORE refactoring/moving a function (L-057)."""
    frappe.db.rollback()
    from rq.registry import FailedJobRegistry
    from rq.job import Job
    from frappe.utils.background_jobs import get_queue

    results = []
    for name in ("short", "default", "long"):
        q = get_queue(name)
        reg = FailedJobRegistry(queue=q)
        for jid in reg.get_job_ids(0, 200):
            try:
                j = Job.fetch(jid, connection=q.connection)
                fn = j.func_name or ""
                if func_name_pattern in fn:
                    results.append({
                        "queue": name,
                        "ended_at": str(j.ended_at),
                        "func": fn,
                        "exc_excerpt": (j.exc_info or "")[:400].replace("\n", " | "),
                    })
            except Exception:
                pass
        if len(results) >= limit:
            break

    if verbose:
        print(f"\nFailed jobs matching '{func_name_pattern}': {len(results)}")
        for r in results[:limit]:
            print(f"  [{r['queue']}] {r['ended_at']}  {r['func']}")
            print(f"    {r['exc_excerpt'][:300]}")
    return results[:limit]


def scheduled_crons(verbose: bool = True) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """List SP scheduled jobs. Use to verify `bench migrate` registered
    new scheduler_events entries (L-049)."""
    frappe.db.rollback()
    rows = frappe.db.sql(
        """
        SELECT name, method, cron_format, stopped, frequency
          FROM "tabScheduled Job Type"
         WHERE method LIKE 'tap_lms.%'
         ORDER BY method
        """,
        as_dict=True,
    )
    if verbose:
        print(f"\nSP-related Scheduled Job Type rows: {len(rows)}")
        for r in rows:
            mark = "✓" if not r["stopped"] else "✗ STOPPED"
            print(f"  {mark}  {r['method']}")
            print(f"      cron={r['cron_format'] or '-'}  "
                  f"freq={r['frequency'] or '-'}")
    return rows


# ── Glific contact-field inspection ─────────────────────────────

def glific_fields(glific_id: str, keys: Optional[List[str]] = None,
                  verbose: bool = True) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Fetch SP-managed contact fields for a Glific contact."""
    if keys is None:
        keys = _SP_CONTACT_FIELDS_DEFAULT
    fields = _fetch_glific_contact_full(glific_id)
    out = {}
    for k in keys:
        v = fields.get(k)
        if isinstance(v, dict):
            out[k] = {"value": v.get("value"),
                      "inserted_at": v.get("inserted_at")}
        else:
            out[k] = v
    if verbose:
        print(f"\nGlific contact {glific_id} — {len(out)} fields:")
        for k in keys:
            entry = out.get(k)
            if isinstance(entry, dict):
                print(f"  {k:32s} = {entry['value']!r:15s}  "
                      f"(set {entry['inserted_at']})")
            else:
                marker = "✗ MISSING" if entry is None else ""
                print(f"  {k:32s} = {entry!r}  {marker}")
    return out


# ── Private helpers ─────────────────────────────────────────────

_SP_CONTACT_FIELDS_DEFAULT = [
    # 7 identity
    "student_id", "student_name", "batch_id", "archetype",
    "language_id", "experiment_arm", "course_level",
    # 11 base state
    "resolved_flow_state", "current_week", "current_path", "current_tier",
