    "program_status", "total_points", "current_streak", "grace_window_end_at",
    "current_expected_submission_type", "last_escalation_step", "submission_count",
    # 9 gamification + 1 computed
    "total_activity_points", "weekly_activity_points",
    "total_quiz_points", "weekly_quiz_points",
    "total_submission_points", "weekly_submission_points",
    "special_gems", "weekly_submission_done", "bonus_quiz_points",
    "weekly_engagement_points",
    # 2 CR-003 escalation routing
    "escalation_order", "escalation_type",
]


def _fetch_glific_contact_full(glific_id: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    if not glific_id:
        return {}
    try:
        from tap_lms.glific_integration import (
            get_glific_settings, get_glific_auth_headers,
        )
        settings = get_glific_settings()
        r = requests.post(
            f"{settings.api_url}/api",
            json={
                "query": "query c($id: ID!){contact(id:$id){contact{id fields}}}",
                "variables": {"id": str(glific_id)},
            },
            headers=get_glific_auth_headers(), timeout=15,
        ).json()
        raw = (r.get("data") or {}).get("contact", {}).get("contact", {}).get("fields")
        return json.loads(raw) if isinstance(raw, str) else (raw or {})
    except Exception:
        return {}


def _fetch_glific_contact(glific_id: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    raw_fields = _fetch_glific_contact_full(glific_id)
    out = {}
    for k, v in raw_fields.items():
        out[k] = v.get("value") if isinstance(v, dict) else v
    return out


def _call_get_student_state(student_id: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    from tap_lms.summer_program.program_enrollment_api import get_student_state
    frappe.local.response = frappe._dict({})
    get_student_state(student_id)
    return dict(frappe.local.response)

docs.title: Frappe client script skill
docs.text: Client scripts run in the desk (the back-office UI) on top of Frappe's form framework. The entry point is a sibling .js file next to the DocType JSON, or a Client Script record stored in the DB. File-based wins for version control; DB-based wins for hot-fixes and per-site overrides.

docs.title: Two scopes
docs.text:
• Form Script — runs on a single document's form view. frappe.ui.form.on("Course Enrollment", { ... }).
  • List View — runs on the list page. frappe.listview_settings["Course Enrollment"] = { ... }.

There are also frappe.ui.Dialog, report scripts (<report>.js), and Web Form scripts. All speak the same frm/frappe API.

docs.title: Form script anatomy
docs.text:
frappe.ui.form.on("Course Enrollment", {
    refresh(frm) {
        // Runs every time the form is rendered (load, after save, after switching tabs back).
        if (frm.doc.docstatus === 1 && frm.doc.status === "Active") {
            frm.add_custom_button(__("Mark Completed"), () => mark_completed(frm), __("Actions"));
        }
        toggle_certificate_section(frm);
    },

    student(frm) {
        // Runs when the `student` field changes.
        if (!frm.doc.student) return;
        frappe.db.get_value("Student", frm.doc.student, "preferred_language")
            .then(({ message }) => frm.set_value("language", message?.preferred_language));
    },

    validate(frm) {
        // Browser-side validation. Server `validate` still runs — this is for fast UX feedback.
        if (frm.doc.start_date && frm.doc.end_date && frm.doc.start_date > frm.doc.end_date) {
            frappe.throw(__("End date must be after start date"));
        }
    },
});

function toggle_certificate_section(frm) {
    frm.toggle_display("certificate_section", frm.doc.status === "Completed");
}

function mark_completed(frm) {
    frappe.call({
        method: "tap_lms.api.complete_enrollment",
        args: { enrollment: frm.doc.name },
        freeze: true,
        freeze_message: __("Wrapping up..."),
    }).then(() => frm.reload_doc());
}

The handler keys are: field event names (fires when that field changes), lifecycle events (refresh, setup, onload, validate, before_save, before_submit, before_cancel), and child-table events (<table_field>_add, <table_field>_remove).

docs.title: The frm object — what you actually use
docs.text:
• frm.doc — the current document as a JS object. Mutate via setters, not direct assignment.
  • frm.set_value(field, value) — write to a field; triggers field events and dirty state.
  • frm.set_df_property(field, prop, value) — change a field property on the fly (reqd, read_only, hidden, options).
  • frm.toggle_display(field, condition) / toggle_enable / toggle_reqd — common patterns one-linered.
  • frm.add_custom_button(label, action, group) — adds to the top toolbar; group collapses related buttons under a menu.
  • frm.dashboard.add_indicator(label, color) — pill on the top of the form.
  • frm.refresh_field("table_field") — re-render a child table after programmatic changes.
  • frm.reload_doc() — fetch fresh server state.
  • frm.is_dirty() / frm.dirty() — track unsaved changes.

docs.title: Calling the server
docs.text:
frappe.call({ method, args, freeze }) is the primary RPC. The method must be a whitelisted Python method (@frappe.whitelist()) reachable by dotted path. For DocType methods, use doc: frm.doc, method: "do_thing" to invoke a controller method.

For lookups, prefer the convenience helpers — they're cheaper than a full frappe.call:

frappe.db.get_value("Course", course_name, "title");
frappe.db.get_doc("Course", course_name);
frappe.db.get_list("Course Enrollment", { filters: { student }, fields: ["name", "status"] });
frappe.db.exists("Course Enrollment", { student, course });
frappe.db.count("Lesson Progress", { enrollment });

docs.title: fetch_from — the lazy man's auto-populate
docs.text:
Don't write a JS handler to copy a field from a linked doc — declare fetch_from in the DocType JSON instead:

{ "fieldname": "course_title", "fieldtype": "Data", "fetch_from": "course.title", "read_only": 1 }

Frappe handles the fetch automatically on the course field's change. Use JS only for transformations the JSON can't express.

docs.title: Dialogs
docs.text:
const dialog = new frappe.ui.Dialog({
    title: __("Award Certificate"),
    fields: [
        { fieldname: "issue_date", fieldtype: "Date", label: __("Issue Date"), default: frappe.datetime.get_today(), reqd: 1 },
        { fieldname: "remarks", fieldtype: "Small Text", label: __("Remarks") },
    ],
    primary_action_label: __("Award"),
    primary_action(values) {
        frappe.call({
            method: "tap_lms.api.award_certificate",
            args: { enrollment: frm.doc.name, ...values },
        }).then(() => { dialog.hide(); frm.reload_doc(); });
    },
});
dialog.show();

docs.title: List view tweaks
docs.text:
frappe.listview_settings["Course Enrollment"] = {
    add_fields: ["status", "course", "student"],
    get_indicator(doc) {
        return {
            "Active":    [__("Active"),    "blue",   "status,=,Active"],
            "Completed": [__("Completed"), "green",  "status,=,Completed"],
            "Dropped":   [__("Dropped"),   "red",    "status,=,Dropped"],
        }[doc.status];
    },
    onload(listview) {
        listview.page.add_inner_button(__("Bulk Activate"), () => bulk_activate(listview));
    },
};

add_fields ensures the fields are in the row payload — without it, doc.status is undefined in get_indicator.

docs.title: Translation
docs.text: Always wrap UI strings in __("..."). Frappe extracts these for the translation files. __("Hello {0}", [name]) for interpolation.

docs.title: When NOT to put it in JS
docs.text:
• Authorization checks — never trust the browser. The server validate is the source of truth; client checks are for UX, not security.
  • Complex computations — round-trip to a whitelisted method instead.
  • Anything that needs DB writes — write a server method, call it.

docs.title: Loading order and caching
docs.text: The desk caches .js files aggressively. After editing, run bench --site <site> clear-cache or hit Ctrl-Shift-R in the browser. If you're staring at unchanged behavior, it's the cache — every time.

docs.title: File path
docs.text:
app/<your_app>/<your_module>/doctype/course_enrollment/course_enrollment.js

For scripts that span multiple DocTypes, use app/<your_app>/public/js/<feature>.js and register it via app_include_js in hooks.py (see the frappe-hooks skill).

docs.title: Frappe controller skill
docs.text: The controller is <doctype>.py next to the DocType JSON. It defines a class that subclasses Document and exposes lifecycle methods Frappe calls automatically.

docs.title: Lifecycle order — memorize this
docs.text:
For an insert: autoname → before_insert → validate → before_save → (DB INSERT) → after_insert → on_update

For an update: validate → before_save → (DB UPDATE) → on_update

For a submit: validate → before_save → (DB UPDATE) → on_update → before_submit → (set docstatus=1) → on_submit

For a cancel: before_cancel → (set docstatus=2) → on_cancel → on_update_after_submit

For a delete: on_trash → (DB DELETE) → after_delete

Pick the right hook. validate is for guarding writes (raise if data is bad). on_update is for side effects that need the doc to already exist in DB (creating linked records, sending emails). before_save is rare — prefer validate.

docs.title: Skeleton
docs.text:
import frappe
from frappe.model.document import Document
from frappe import _


class CourseEnrollment(Document):
    def validate(self):
        self._guard_duplicate_enrollment()
        self._set_default_status()

    def on_submit(self):
        self._notify_student()
        self._create_progress_record()

    def on_cancel(self):
        # Reverse anything on_submit did.
        frappe.db.set_value(
            "Lesson Progress",
            {"enrollment": self.name},
            "status", "Cancelled",
        )

    # --- private helpers -------------------------------------------

    def _guard_duplicate_enrollment(self):
        if frappe.db.exists(
            "Course Enrollment",
            {"student": self.student, "course": self.course, "name": ("!=", self.name)},
        ):
            frappe.throw(_("{0} is already enrolled in {1}").format(self.student, self.course))

    def _set_default_status(self):
        if not self.status:
            self.status = "Active"

    def _notify_student(self):
        # ...
        pass

    def _create_progress_record(self):
        # ...
        pass

Use leading-underscore helpers to keep the public surface clean. Frappe only calls methods named after lifecycle events; everything else is yours.

docs.title: Raising errors the right way
docs.text:
frappe.throw(_("message")) aborts the transaction and shows the message to the user. frappe.msgprint(_("...")) shows a non-fatal notice. Always wrap user-visible strings in _() for translation. Pass title and indicator for richer UX:

frappe.throw(_("Course is full"), title=_("Cannot enrol"), indicator="red")

Custom exception classes give cleaner programmatic handling:

class CourseFullError(frappe.ValidationError): pass

frappe.throw(_("Course is full"), exc=CourseFullError)

docs.title: Reading and writing data
docs.text:
Inside a controller, the doc itself is self. For other docs:

  • frappe.get_doc("Course", course_name) — full document object, fires controller hooks on save.
  • frappe.get_cached_doc(...) — same but cached for the request. Use for read-only lookups in hot paths.
  • frappe.db.get_value("Course", name, "title") — single-field read, no controller. Fast.
  • frappe.db.get_value("Course", {"code": "CS101"}, ["title", "credits"], as_dict=True) — filter + multi-field.
  • frappe.get_all("Course Enrollment", filters={"student": self.student}, fields=["name", "status"]) — multi-row read; respects user permissions if ignore_permissions not set.
  • frappe.db.sql("SELECT ...", values, as_dict=True) — escape hatch. Use parameterized queries; never f-string user input.
  • frappe.db.set_value("Course", name, "status", "Closed") — single-field write, does not fire controller hooks. Use sparingly; prefer loading the doc and calling .save() so validation runs.

docs.title: Permissions inside the controller
docs.text:
Controllers run with the caller's permissions by default. To bypass (e.g., a student submission needs to update an instructor's record), pass ignore_permissions=True to .save() / .insert(), or run the work inside frappe.flags overrides. Be deliberate — bypassing is the #1 source of authorization bugs.

note = frappe.new_doc("Communication")
note.subject = f"New enrollment from {self.student}"
note.insert(ignore_permissions=True)

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text: Each request runs in a single transaction; Frappe commits on success and rolls back on exception. Avoid manually calling frappe.db.commit() inside controller code — it breaks atomicity. The exceptions are background jobs and long migrations, where partial commits are intentional.

docs.title: Background work
docs.text:
on_submit should not block the user for >100ms. Anything heavy (PDF rendering, external API calls, sending many emails) goes in frappe.enqueue:

def on_submit(self):
    frappe.enqueue(
        "tap_lms.tap_lms.doctype.course_enrollment.course_enrollment.send_welcome_packet",
        enrollment=self.name,
        queue="long",
        job_name=f"welcome:{self.name}",
    )

The function must be importable by dotted path (so module-level, not a method on self). Pass primitive args.

docs.title: Background jobs — log structured context on BOTH paths
docs.text:
Background jobs (frappe.enqueue targets, scheduler functions) that swallow exceptions silently are the #1 source of "but the queue says success" debugging pain on this project. Filed as bugs #3 and #5 (both 2026-05-18): _process_pe_chunk silently rejected 4 of 41 PE creations and _sync_contact_fields_job intermittently dropped field writes — neither left an Error Log entry, both took hours of console diagnostics to find.

Hard rule for any background job:

  1. Every try/except must log via frappe.log_error(title=..., message=...) with structured context: PE name, student ID, glific ID, batch name, the action that was attempted, the underlying exception type + message.
  2. The success path must log via frappe.logger().info(...) with at minimum "what worker ran, what entity, what changed." This is what lets ops answer "did this contact actually receive the field update?" without running custom diagnostic queries.
  3. Returning silently with no exception AND no log is BLOCKING per code reviewer. Workers must succeed visibly or fail visibly — not both, never neither.
  4. DLQ patterns (P-007 / L-015) make the silent-success case technically OK only if the success path itself logs as in (2).

docs.title: Wrong pattern
docs.text:
def _sync_contact_fields_job(glific_id, fields, pe_name, ...):
    try:
        update_contact_fields(glific_id, fields)
    except Exception:
        pass   # ← BLOCKING: silent swallow

docs.title: Right pattern
docs.text:
def _sync_contact_fields_job(glific_id, fields, pe_name, ...):
    try:
        update_contact_fields(glific_id, fields)
        frappe.logger().info(
            f"sync_contact_fields_ok: pe={pe_name} glific={glific_id} "
            f"fields_count={len(fields)}"
        )
    except Exception as e:
        frappe.log_error(
            title="SP Glific Sync Failed",
            message=(
                f"sync_contact_fields_failed: pe={pe_name} "
                f"glific={glific_id} fields={list(fields.keys())} "
                f"error={type(e).__name__}: {e}"
            ),
        )
        raise   # let the retry/DLQ machinery handle re-enqueue

Use a structured log-key prefix (e.g. sync_contact_fields_ok / sync_contact_fields_failed) so ops can grep for either outcome.

docs.title: External identifier semantics — avoid contact_id ↔ student_id confusion
docs.text:
The project carries multiple distinct kinds of identifiers that share variable names across functions. Confusing them is a recurring source of "Glific returned a generic error" bugs (2026-05-19 FeedbackConsumer.send_glific_notification shipped passing Student.name as contact_id; bug took 2 hours to debug).

Identifier Type Example Lives on Frappe Student doc name string "ST00051238" Student.name, PE.student Glific contact ID numeric string "13325" Student.glific_id, PE.glific_id, Glific contactByPhone result Phone (Glific-stored) E.164-ish "91XXXXXXXXXX" Student.phone, Glific contact's .phone Frappe Batch doc name string "palv2-test-BT52231" Batch.name, PE.batch Friendly batch identifier short string "SP_BATCH_01" Batch.batch_id, Glific batch_id contact field

docs.title: Hard rules
docs.text:
1. Any function whose signature includes contact_id, glific_id, student_id, batch, or batch_id must document in its docstring exactly which of these identifier types it expects.
  2. When crossing between systems (Glific ↔ Frappe), explicitly resolve the identifier at the call site rather than passing it through opaquely.
  3. Any call to a Glific API helper (start_contact_flow, update_contact_fields, add_contact_to_group, remove_contact_from_group) must visibly resolve the Glific contact ID at the call site — not via a variable named student_id whose origin is ambiguous.

docs.title: Wrong pattern
docs.text:
def send_glific_notification(self, message_data):
    student_id = message_data.get("student_id")   # actually a Frappe doc name
    start_contact_flow(
        flow_id=flow_id,
        contact_id=student_id,   # ← Glific can't resolve "ST00051238"
        default_results=...,
    )

docs.title: Right pattern
docs.text:
def send_glific_notification(self, message_data):
    student_id = message_data.get("student_id")   # Frappe Student doc name
    glific_id = frappe.db.get_value("Student", student_id, "glific_id")
    if not glific_id:
        frappe.logger().warning(
            f"Student {student_id} has no glific_id; "
            f"skipping notification for submission {submission_id}"
        )
        return
    start_contact_flow(
        flow_id=str(flow_id),
        contact_id=str(glific_id),   # ← visibly resolved at the call site
        default_results=...,
    )

docs.title: Code-reviewer rule
docs.text: When reviewing any call to a Glific API helper, ask: "where did the contact_id come from?" If the answer is "a parameter that flowed in from a few functions ago" — flag it as Major. The variable name student_id is opaque about which kind of ID it carries; trace it to its origin or require an explicit resolution at the call site.

docs.title: Realtime updates
docs.text: frappe.publish_realtime("event_name", {"payload": 1}, user=self.owner) pushes a SocketIO event the JS form listens for. Useful for "your certificate is ready" type pings.

docs.title: State-machine controllers — project idioms
docs.text: For controllers that mutate a state-machine doc (ProgramEnrollment and friends), three patterns are non-negotiable on this project. They live canonically in .claude/memory/patterns.md:

docs.title: Atomic claim with journey_label guard (P-001)
docs.text:
Every state-changing UPDATE goes through a WHERE journey_label = expected_label … RETURNING name query. 0 rows returned = parallel handler already moved the state; skip without raising.

claimed = frappe.db.sql("""
    UPDATE "tabProgramEnrollment"
       SET resolved_flow_state = %s, journey_label = %s,
           next_action_at = %s,    next_action_type = %s
     WHERE name = %s AND journey_label = %s
     RETURNING name
""", (new_state, new_label, next_at, next_type, pe_name, expected_label))
if not claimed:
    return

Never use SELECT ROW_COUNT() to count affected rows — Postgres doesn't have it (lesson L-001). Use len(claimed) or if not claimed:.

docs.title: COALESCE-update for race-tolerant counters (P-002)
docs.text:
Counters that race against resets (weekly point counters reset by T14, etc.) MUST use a single atomic UPDATE with COALESCE, never read-then-write:

# Bad — read-then-write loses races
pe = frappe.get_doc("Program Enrollment", pe_name)
pe.weekly_quiz_points += earned
pe.save()

# Good — atomic at the column level
frappe.db.sql("""
    UPDATE "tabProgramEnrollment"
       SET weekly_quiz_points = COALESCE(weekly_quiz_points, 0) + %s
     WHERE name = %s
""", (earned, pe_name))

Lesson L-011.

docs.title: The wider rule — doc.save(ignore_permissions=True) is a write-every-column hazard
docs.text:
pe.save(ignore_permissions=True) writes the FULL row from the in-memory doc. Any column another path bumped via atomic SQL between frappe.get_doc("PE", name) and this .save() gets silently overwritten with the stale value the in-memory doc has been carrying. The longer the request/handler, the wider the race window.

This isn't theoretical: the TAP LMS PE doctype has 40+ columns; ~10 of them (the total_* and weekly_* points columns plus the streak/gems pair) get bumped concurrently by activity_points / quiz_points / feedback hook handlers. Every pe.save() in a code path that doesn't intend to mutate ALL columns is a potential drift source. During the 2026-05-26 pre-launch sweep we found 11 such sites (7 in flow_callback.py, 3 in pe_dispatcher.py, 1 T25 in state_machine.py) and replaced them with targeted db.set_value({...changed fields only...}) + pe.reload().

# WRONG — writes every PE column from a possibly-stale in-memory doc
pe = frappe.get_doc("ProgramEnrollment", pe_name)
# ... long handler runs; another worker bumps total_points concurrently ...
pe.next_action_at = some_new_time
pe.next_action_type = "escalation"
pe.save(ignore_permissions=True)   # ← clobbers the concurrent total_points bump

# RIGHT — atomic, only touches the columns this handler owns
frappe.db.set_value(
    "ProgramEnrollment", pe_name,
    {"next_action_at": some_new_time, "next_action_type": "escalation"},
    update_modified=False,
)
pe.reload()    # if downstream code in this handler needs to read pe fields

Rule of thumb for PE-like doctypes with concurrent column writers: handlers that intend to write 1–3 specific fields use db.set_value; handlers that intend to bulk-reset the whole row (dev_tools.reset_pe_to_state_0) keep pe.save() because the intent IS to clobber. The signal is the verb: "set N specific things" vs "rewrite the whole doc to a known state."

db.set_value bypasses controller validate AND on_update AND track_changes — this is the standard Frappe behavior. It's a deliberate trade: the gain is no-clobber semantics; the cost is no automatic save-hook side effects. If the column being set is Glific-mirrored, follow up with dev_tools.reconcile_pe_to_glific(pe_name) (or _enqueue_contact_field_sync(pe)) to push the change. If the column requires validate-style guarding, do the validation manually before calling set_value.

docs.title: Audit-field-first idempotency (P-005)
docs.text:
Per-attempt audit fields (e.g., StudentQuizAttempt.points_earned) should be written FIRST, before any rollup updates. The field is the lock — re-runs check if attempt.points_earned: return.

def award_points(attempt_name):
    attempt = frappe.get_doc("Student Quiz Attempt", attempt_name)
    if attempt.points_earned:
        return                     # ← write-once lock; re-runs are no-op
    earned = compute(...)
    frappe.db.set_value("Student Quiz Attempt", attempt_name, "points_earned", earned)
    apply_to_pe_counters(earned)   # safe to retry from here

Lesson L-012.

docs.title: Common anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Putting business rules in before_save instead of validate — they don't run during db_update calls and you get inconsistent behavior.
  • Using frappe.db.set_value to flip a status field that has its own controller logic, then being surprised the side effects didn't fire.
  • Querying inside a loop (for x in ...: frappe.get_doc(...)) — fetch once with frappe.get_all and a name in (...) filter.
  • Forgetting _() on strings, then having the translation team chase you.
  • Calling frappe.db.commit() in the middle of on_submit — partial state if the rest of the method throws.
  • Wrapping a state-changing UPDATE in a broad except Exception: block with a "MariaDB fallback" branch. The except swallows real PG errors, the fallback is dead code on this project, and the combination risks double-running. Lesson L-007 — remove rather than maintain.

docs.title: When the controller is too small for its own file
docs.text: Generic helpers (e.g., a function used by many DocTypes) belong in app/<your_app>/<your_module>/utils.py or a dedicated module — not duplicated across controllers. Import explicitly; don't rely on Frappe's monkey patching.

docs.title: Frappe DocType skill
docs.text: DocTypes are Frappe's data model. A DocType bundles together a database table, a form UI, server-side controller, and permissions in one declarative JSON file plus a sibling Python module.

docs.title: When to use which mechanism
docs.text:
Three ways to extend the data model — pick correctly, this is where most Frappe projects go wrong.

  • New DocType in your custom app — for entities your app owns (e.g., Course Enrollment, Lesson Progress). Lives in app/<your_app>/<your_module>/doctype/<doctype_name>/. Editable by developers, version-controlled.
  • Custom Field on a core DocType — adds a single field to ERPNext-owned DocTypes (Customer, Item, User). Stored as Custom Field records, fixtures-exportable. Use when the field is conceptually "ours" but lives on a foreign DocType.
  • Customize Form / Property Setter — change properties of existing fields (label, reqd, hidden, default). Stored as Property Setter records. Don't use to add fields — that's Custom Field's job.

If you're tempted to fork or directly edit a core DocType JSON, stop — it'll get blown away on next bench update. Use Custom Fields.

docs.title: Anatomy of a DocType folder
docs.text:
<your_app>/<your_module>/doctype/course_enrollment/
├── __init__.py
├── course_enrollment.json     # schema + UI definition
├── course_enrollment.py       # controller (server-side)
├── course_enrollment.js       # client script (browser-side, optional)
├── test_course_enrollment.py  # unit tests
└── course_enrollment_dashboard.py  # dashboard config (optional)

The naming is strict: snake_case folder + matching filenames. The name field inside the JSON is the human "Course Enrollment".

docs.title: Field types worth knowing
docs.text:
Data (short text), Small Text / Long Text / Text Editor (rich), Int, Float, Currency, Percent, Date, Datetime, Time, Check (boolean), Select (dropdown with options newline-separated), Link (foreign key — options is the target DocType), Dynamic Link (target chosen at runtime via another field), Table (child table — options is child DocType), Table MultiSelect (many-to-many sugar), Attach / Attach Image, Code / JSON, Password (encrypted at rest), Geolocation, Color, Signature.

For LMS-style work in TAP LMS, the common patterns are: Link to Course, Student, Instructor; Table for lesson lists, attempt logs, rubric rows; Select for status fields; Datetime for scheduling.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
The naming_rule plus autoname field decide how new docs get their primary key. Pick one consciously:

  • field:<fieldname> — name = value of that field (must be unique). Good for human-meaningful names like course codes.
  • naming_series: plus a naming_series Select field — ENROLL-.YYYY.-.#### style. Best default for transactional records.
  • format: — Jinja-ish template, e.g. {course}-{student}.
  • Prompt — user types it.
  • Autoincrement — Postgres bigserial. Fast, opaque, no sortable meaning.
  • hash — random. Use for high-write-concurrency doctypes (see warning below); avoid otherwise if a meaningful name is cheap.

For TAP LMS, prefer naming series for enrollments/attempts/progress (audit-friendly) and field: for catalog items like Course (uses course_code).

Counter-autoname (format:...{####} / naming_series:) serializes concurrent inserts — never use it on a hot, webhook-driven doctype. Every {####} insert takes FOR UPDATE on the shared tabSeries.current row. Under concurrent Glific-webhook dispatch this produces psycopg2.errors.SerializationFailure: could not serialize access due to concurrent update, which then cascades via the L-030 poisoned-txn path into a Glific 400. The 2026-06-04 trainer-cohort incident (BR-003) hit this on StudentStageProgress insert from get_next_content. Fix: use hash autoname (no shared counter → contention disappears at the source) for any doctype inserted on the request path of a high-concurrency endpoint. Hash and format names coexist within one doctype, so converting is safe as long as nothing constructs or parses the .name (lookups must be by field filter or stored .name). See L-075.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Edit permissions array directly in the JSON, or use the Role Permission Manager UI and export as fixture. Match each row to a Role, set read/write/create/delete/submit/cancel/amend flags, and set permlevel (0 = whole doc, higher levels = field-level locks via the field's permlevel).

User Permissions further restrict by linked record (e.g., "this instructor only sees their own Courses") and are applied at runtime — set apply_user_permissions on relevant Link fields.

docs.title: Submittable vs not
docs.text: Setting is_submittable: 1 gives you the submit/cancel/amend lifecycle (docstatus 0=draft, 1=submitted, 2=cancelled). Use for accounting-shaped data where audit trail matters (attempts, certifications, payments). Don't use for plain CRUD records — adds friction with no upside.

docs.title: After every schema change
docs.text: The schema only goes live after bench --site <site> migrate. Without migrate, the form looks updated but the Postgres table is stale and writes will silently drop new fields. Always run migrate (or remind the user to) after editing a DocType JSON.

docs.title: Editing JSON safely
docs.text:
Order matters less than you'd think — Frappe sorts field order from the idx value, not the array position. But: keep module, name, engine, creation untouched unless you know what you're doing. Don't hand-edit the modified timestamp; let Frappe rewrite it.

When generating new DocType JSON, model it after one of the existing DocTypes in app/<your_app>/<your_module>/doctype/ — copy a sibling, then change name, fields, permissions. Frappe is finicky about the exact key names.

docs.title: Child tables
docs.text: A child DocType has istable: 1 and no permissions of its own — it inherits from the parent. The parent declares the relationship with a Table field whose options points at the child. Don't try to query a child table directly via frappe.get_all without filtering by parent and parenttype, or you'll get rows from every parent that uses this child type.

docs.title: Single DocType
docs.text: Setting issingle: 1 makes a settings-style record — exactly one row, addressed by name = DocType name (e.g., "TAP LMS Settings"). Stored in tabSingles as key/value rows, not as a regular table. Use for app-wide config.

docs.title: Reference: minimal JSON shape
docs.text:
{
  "doctype": "DocType",
  "name": "Course Enrollment",
  "module": "TAP LMS",
  "engine": "InnoDB",
  "naming_rule": "By \"Naming Series\" field",
  "autoname": "naming_series:",
  "fields": [
    {"fieldname": "naming_series", "fieldtype": "Select", "label": "Series",
     "options": "ENROLL-.YYYY.-.#####", "reqd": 1},
    {"fieldname": "student", "fieldtype": "Link", "options": "Student", "reqd": 1, "in_list_view": 1},
    {"fieldname": "course", "fieldtype": "Link", "options": "Course", "reqd": 1, "in_list_view": 1},
    {"fieldname": "enrolled_on", "fieldtype": "Datetime", "default": "now"},
    {"fieldname": "status", "fieldtype": "Select", "options": "Active\nCompleted\nDropped", "default": "Active", "in_list_view": 1}
  ],
  "permissions": [
    {"role": "TAP Instructor", "read": 1, "write": 1, "create": 1, "delete": 0},
    {"role": "TAP Student", "read": 1}
  ]
}

(Note engine: "InnoDB" is harmless on Postgres — Frappe keeps the field for compatibility.)

docs.title: Postgres caveat
docs.text: Frappe creates the table via its own migration code, not raw CREATE TABLE. Field name collisions with Postgres reserved words (e.g. user, order, group) will cause grief — Frappe quotes table names but not always inside ad-hoc joins. Avoid those names where possible; if forced, expect to debug an occasional psycopg2.errors.SyntaxError and consult the frappe-postgres skill.

docs.title: Frappe hooks.py skill
docs.text: hooks.py lives at app/<your_app>/hooks.py and is the single declarative configuration file Frappe reads at startup. Every "react to X happening anywhere in the system" extension goes here.

docs.title: When hooks vs. when controllers
docs.text:
Use a controller method (<doctype>.py lifecycle hook) when reacting to events on your own DocType. The controller is the home for that doc's logic.

Use hooks.py doc_events when reacting to events on a DocType you don't own — typically a core ERPNext DocType (User, Customer, Sales Invoice) or one from another app. You can't edit their controllers, so you register a callback in hooks.py.

docs.title: doc_events
docs.text:
doc_events = {
    "User": {
        "after_insert": "tap_lms.tap_lms.user_hooks.create_student_profile",
    },
    "Sales Invoice": {
        "on_submit": [
            "tap_lms.tap_lms.billing_hooks.activate_paid_enrollments",
            "tap_lms.tap_lms.billing_hooks.send_receipt",
        ],
    },
    "*": {
        "before_save": "tap_lms.tap_lms.audit.stamp_modified_by_ip",
    },
}

Each value is a dotted import path to a function. Signature: def handler(doc, method=None): where doc is the document and method is the event name (useful when one function listens to multiple events).

"*" matches every DocType. Use sparingly — it runs on every save in the system.

docs.title: Scheduler events
docs.text:
scheduler_events = {
    "all":     ["tap_lms.tap_lms.scheduled.heartbeat"],         # every ~4 minutes
    "hourly":  ["tap_lms.tap_lms.scheduled.refresh_summaries"],
    "daily":   ["tap_lms.tap_lms.scheduled.expire_lapsed_enrollments"],
    "weekly":  ["tap_lms.tap_lms.scheduled.send_weekly_digest"],
    "monthly": ["tap_lms.tap_lms.scheduled.archive_old_attempts"],
    "cron": {
        "0 2 * * *": ["tap_lms.tap_lms.scheduled.nightly_sync"],
    },
}

cron keys take standard 5-field crontab expressions. Functions take no arguments. Errors are logged to the Error Log DocType; they don't kill the scheduler.

For the scheduler to actually run, the bench daemon must be up. In dev: bench start. In prod: supervisor should be running bench schedule and bench worker --queue default,short,long.

Critical: changes to scheduler_events require bench migrate, not just bench restart. Frappe stores scheduler entries in the tabScheduled Job Type table; that table is populated from hooks.scheduler_events only by migrate. A new cron entry added to hooks.py after restart-only deploys is invisible to the scheduler — the function never fires. Verify with:

import frappe; frappe.db.rollback()
frappe.db.sql("""
    SELECT method, cron_format, stopped FROM "tabScheduled Job Type"
     WHERE method LIKE 'your_app.your_module.%' ORDER BY method
""", as_dict=True)

This contrasts with doc_events, override_doctype_class, and other hooks.py keys that take effect on bench restart alone because they're read at code-import time.

docs.title: Background jobs via frappe.enqueue — the silent-success failure mode
docs.text:
Functions you call with frappe.enqueue(method_path, queue="short", **kwargs) run in RQ workers. Two things to know:

1. Queues and priorities. Standard queues are short (high priority, jobs < ~30s), default (medium), long (low, multi-minute). Workers typically poll multiple queues; short jobs interleave fastest. Use short for per-user-event work (Glific sync, content-log inserts) and long for slow API calls (Vocallabs, AI feedback).

2. The silent-success failure mode. RQ marks a job as failed only if it raises an exception. A job that catches an exception and returns normally is marked finished — the FailedJobRegistry stays empty, queue-depth alerts stay silent, but the work the job was supposed to do never happened.

# WRONG — looks "finished" to RQ even when the insert fails
def my_job(student_id, content_id, ...):
    try:
        log.insert(ignore_permissions=True)
        frappe.db.commit()
    except Exception as e:
        frappe.log_error(f"job failed: {e}", "My App")
        # implicit return None → RQ thinks the job succeeded

# RIGHT — fails loudly so RQ + FailedJobRegistry + ops see it
def my_job(student_id, content_id, ...):
    try:
        log.insert(ignore_permissions=True)
        frappe.db.commit()
    except Exception as e:
        try:
            frappe.db.rollback()    # L-030: clears poisoned txn so log_error works
        except Exception:
            pass
        try:
            frappe.log_error(
                f"my_job failed: {e}\nstudent={student_id} content={content_id}",
                "My App",
            )
        except Exception:
            frappe.logger().error(f"my_job failed (log_error also failed): {e}")
        raise   # ← critical: marks the job FAILED in RQ

Two corollaries: - Rollback before log_error. Postgres aborts the whole transaction on the first failed statement; frappe.log_error does its own SELECT and would fail with InFailedSqlTransaction without the rollback. The nested try/except around log_error itself is a defense against double-fault when the Error Log doctype meta lookup also fails. - Pair the raise with retry+DLQ if the job is idempotent. Pattern P-007: enqueue the job again with retry_count + 1 until a MAX_RETRIES budget is exhausted, then write a structured DLQ Error Log entry for manual replay. state_machine._sync_contact_fields_job is the canonical implementation.

Before moving / renaming an existing background job, search its failure history first:

# After loading sp_console (see skills/frappe-bench/SKILL.md console section):
queue_failures_for("the_func_name")

If there are hits, fix the root cause inline before relocating. A function being moved usually triggers a code review; a silent-failure bug being moved unchanged turns into a launch-week incident.

docs.title: fixtures
docs.text:
Fixtures are records exported as JSON and re-imported on bench migrate — used for Roles, Custom Fields, Property Setters, Workflows, Print Formats, anything you want to ship as part of the app.

fixtures = [
    {"dt": "Custom Field", "filters": [["dt", "in", ["User", "Customer"]]]},
    {"dt": "Property Setter", "filters": [["doc_type", "in", ["User", "Customer"]]]},
    {"dt": "Role", "filters": [["name", "in", ["TAP Instructor", "TAP Student"]]]},
    "Workflow",
    "Workflow State",
    "Workflow Action Master",
]

Export with bench --site <site> export-fixtures. The JSON files land in app/<your_app>/fixtures/. Commit them.

docs.title: JS / CSS includes
docs.text:
# Loaded on every desk page
app_include_js = ["/assets/tap_lms/js/desk.bundle.js"]
app_include_css = ["/assets/tap_lms/css/desk.bundle.css"]

# Loaded on every portal/web page
web_include_js = ["/assets/tap_lms/js/portal.bundle.js"]
web_include_css = ["/assets/tap_lms/css/portal.bundle.css"]

# Loaded only on a specific DocType's form (alternative to a sibling .js file)
doctype_js = {"Sales Invoice": "public/js/sales_invoice_overrides.js"}
doctype_list_js = {"Sales Invoice": "public/js/sales_invoice_list.js"}

For bundled assets, drop .bundle.js files in public/js/ and Frappe's esbuild step picks them up on bench build.

docs.title: Override classes (the nuclear option)
docs.text:
override_doctype_class = {
    "Sales Invoice": "tap_lms.tap_lms.overrides.sales_invoice.CustomSalesInvoice",
}

The override class subclasses the original. Use only when you need to change behavior the original doesn't expose via lifecycle hooks. Test it on every Frappe upgrade — overrides are the most upgrade-fragile thing in hooks.py.

override_whitelisted_methods = {
    "frappe.www.contact.send_message": "tap_lms.tap_lms.overrides.contact.send_message",
}

docs.title: Permission queries (row-level filtering)
docs.text:
permission_query_conditions = {
    "Course Enrollment": "tap_lms.tap_lms.permissions.enrollment_query",
}

has_permission = {
    "Course Enrollment": "tap_lms.tap_lms.permissions.enrollment_has_permission",
}

The query function returns a SQL fragment Frappe AND's into list queries. The has_permission function returns a bool for individual doc access.

def enrollment_query(user):
    if "TAP Admin" in frappe.get_roles(user): return ""
    return f"`tabCourse Enrollment`.owner = {frappe.db.escape(user)}"

(That backtick syntax is the one place Frappe's translator handles for you. On Postgres it becomes "tabCourse Enrollment".owner.)

docs.title: Install / migrate / uninstall lifecycle
docs.text:
before_install = "tap_lms.install.before_install"
after_install = "tap_lms.install.after_install"
after_migrate = ["tap_lms.install.create_default_roles"]
before_uninstall = "tap_lms.install.cleanup"

after_install runs once per site when the app is first installed; after_migrate runs on every bench migrate. Idempotency matters — wrap in if not frappe.db.exists(...).

docs.title: Patches
docs.text: Schema changes that need data migration go in patches.txt (one dotted path per line) and the patch lives at app/<your_app>/patches/<version>/<name>.py with an execute() function. Patches run in order, each only once. Use them whenever you rename fields, change types non-trivially, or backfill data.

docs.title: Email and notifications
docs.text:
notification_config = "tap_lms.notifications.get_notification_config"

The function returns a dict that drives the bell-icon notifications in the desk. Useful for "you have N pending grading items" indicators.

docs.title: Boot session
docs.text:
boot_session = "tap_lms.boot.boot_session"

Inject keys into the JS frappe.boot object that's available on every page. Useful for global config the front-end needs (feature flags, branding).

docs.title: What NOT to put in hooks.py
docs.text:
• Long imports at module level — hooks.py is read on every request indirectly via the metadata cache. Keep it dependency-light.
  • Complex logic — it's a config file. Functions belong elsewhere; hooks.py only references their dotted paths.
  • Conditional blocks based on environment — Frappe doesn't reload hooks.py on env changes; you'll surprise yourself. Use frappe.conf.get(...) inside the called functions instead.

docs.title: After editing hooks.py
docs.text:
Hooks are cached. After changes:

bench --site <site> clear-cache
bench restart   # or `bench start` in dev

Without this, your new doc_events / scheduler entries won't fire and you'll spend an hour blaming the wrong code.

docs.title: Frappe + PostgreSQL skill
docs.text: Frappe was born MariaDB-first; Postgres support landed later and is fully functional but riddled with small differences. Most Frappe code runs the same; raw SQL and a handful of operations don't.

docs.title: Quick rule
docs.text: Whenever you write SQL, ask: would this work on Postgres? Most copy-pasted Frappe ERPNext SQL was written against MariaDB and will quietly fail or behave differently on PG.

docs.title: Identifier quoting
docs.text:
MariaDB uses backticks: `tabCourse`. Postgres uses double quotes: "tabCourse". Frappe's frappe.db.sql translates backticks at runtime, but only inside the bare query string — not inside dynamically built fragments or stored procedures. If you see psycopg2.errors.SyntaxError: syntax error at or near ""`, that's a backtick that didn't get translated.

Safer: write idiomatic Postgres SQL with "..." quoting and let frappe.db.sql pass it through, OR use the query builder (frappe.qb) which is dialect-aware.

docs.title: IFNULL / ISNULL → COALESCE
docs.text:
-- Bad on PG
SELECT IFNULL(grade, 0) FROM "tabAttempt";
-- Good
SELECT COALESCE(grade, 0) FROM "tabAttempt";

docs.title: GROUP_CONCAT → STRING_AGG
docs.text:
-- MariaDB
SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(student SEPARATOR ', ') FROM "tabCourse Enrollment";
-- Postgres
SELECT STRING_AGG(student, ', ') FROM "tabCourse Enrollment";

docs.title: Date math
docs.text: DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 1 DAY) is MariaDB. PG: d + INTERVAL '1 day' or d + 1 for date types. DATEDIFF(a, b) becomes (a::date - b::date). NOW() works both places; CURDATE() is MariaDB-only — use CURRENT_DATE.

docs.title: LIMIT x, y → LIMIT y OFFSET x
docs.text: PG doesn't accept the two-argument form.

docs.title: Case sensitivity
docs.text: PG is case-sensitive on identifiers and on string comparisons. WHERE email = 'Foo@Bar.com' won't match foo@bar.com rows. Use ILIKE or LOWER(email) = LOWER(...) and put a functional index on LOWER(email) if you query that way.

docs.title: Boolean
docs.text: PG has a real BOOLEAN type; MariaDB uses TINYINT(1). Frappe's Check field maps to int on both — your queries should compare flag = 1, not flag = TRUE, to stay portable.

docs.title: SELECT ROW_COUNT() does not exist on PG
docs.text:
MariaDB has a session-level ROW_COUNT() you can SELECT after an UPDATE/DELETE to count affected rows. Postgres does not — that query errors out (or, worse on Frappe, returns nothing useful). Two correct alternatives:

# Option A — RETURNING (preferred for UPDATE-claim patterns)
claimed = frappe.db.sql("""
    UPDATE "tabProgramEnrollment"
       SET journey_label = %s
     WHERE name = %s AND journey_label = %s
     RETURNING name
""", (new_label, pe_name, expected_label))
if not claimed:
    return  # 0 rows = somebody else already moved it

# Option B — cursor.rowcount when RETURNING isn't ergonomic
n = frappe.db.sql("UPDATE ... WHERE ...", values)
# frappe.db._cursor.rowcount has the count; usually you want RETURNING instead.

Lesson L-001. Single highest-consequence MariaDB-ism on this project — silently broke an atomic claim in production-bound code (CR-2026-05-10 #B1). When you see SELECT ROW_COUNT() in any patch or controller, treat it as BLOCKING.

docs.title: WHERE col IN %s → WHERE col = ANY(%s) (and the Frappe modify_values gotcha)
docs.text:
The IN %s form with a tuple parameter is a MariaDB/psycopg trick that doesn't always survive on PG (and will silently behave wrong on empty tuples). Use = ANY(%s) with a Python list for portable, robust PG SQL:

# Bad
frappe.db.sql("SELECT name FROM \"tabFoo\" WHERE state IN %s", (("a", "b", "c"),))

# Good
frappe.db.sql("SELECT name FROM \"tabFoo\" WHERE state = ANY(%s)", (["a", "b", "c"],))

Lesson L-005.

Common second-order trap (recurred 3× — pe_dispatcher → migration patch → next patch): Frappe's frappe.db.sql runs the params through modify_values(), which wraps a single-item (list,) tuple oddly. If you write frappe.db.sql("... = ANY(%s::text[])", (legacy_names,)) you'll get op ANY/ALL (array) requires array on right side or malformed array literal at runtime — the tuple-around-list becomes a Postgres composite, not an array. Pick one of these two safe forms and don't mix them:

# Form A — `= ANY(%s)` with a bare list (NOT a tuple wrapping a list)
frappe.db.sql(
    'SELECT name FROM "tabFoo" WHERE state = ANY(%s)',
    ([s for s in states],),       # ← this is the one place the (list,) wrapping is correct
)
# Note: psycopg2 needs the outer tuple as the params iterable. The inner is the actual list.
# In practice, prefer Form B for migration patches — it avoids the cognitive load.

# Form B — `IN %s` with `tuple(list)` (Frappe's canonical Postgres-safe pattern)
frappe.db.sql(
    'UPDATE "tabPGCollection" SET is_active = 0 WHERE parent IN %s',
    (tuple(legacy_bpr_names),),
)

The recurrence (CR-2026-05-15 C1, fixed in commit 561bb5c) was specifically a migration patch that copied the = ANY(%s::text[]) shape from an in-line comment but passed (list,) and got the modify_values mangling. Code-reviewer rule: whenever you see ANY(%s) or ANY(%s::text[]) in raw SQL, immediately check the param shape — if it's (some_list,) where some_list is a Python list of strings/ints, it will fail at runtime. Prefer IN %s + tuple(list) for migration patches.

docs.title: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE → ON CONFLICT
docs.text:
-- PG upsert
INSERT INTO "tabLesson Progress" (name, status)
VALUES (%s, %s)
ON CONFLICT (name) DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status;

docs.title: Full-text search
docs.text: Frappe's LIKE '%foo%' works but is slow. PG has to_tsvector / to_tsquery and GIN indexes — much faster for text search. Frappe's global search uses its own table (__global_search) and works the same on either backend, so prefer it over hand-rolled LIKE queries when possible.

docs.title: JSON fields
docs.text:
Frappe JSON fieldtype is stored as text historically, not jsonb. If you need to query into JSON values, you currently have to cast: (value::jsonb->>'key'). Add a generated column or a separate indexed column if you query the same JSON path repeatedly.

If you want a GIN index on the JSON (for @>, ?, key-existence queries), the column itself must be real jsonb, not text. Convert via patch:

def execute():
    frappe.db.sql_ddl("""
        ALTER TABLE "tabProgramEventLog"
        ALTER COLUMN details TYPE jsonb USING details::jsonb;
    """)
    frappe.db.sql_ddl("""
        CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_eventlog_details
        ON "tabProgramEventLog" USING GIN (details);
    """)

Lesson L-006. Without the USING details::jsonb cast clause, ALTER fails on rows with non-trivial content.

docs.title: Postgres string functions on JSON columns need an explicit ::text cast
docs.text:
-- WORKS
SELECT LEFT(details::text, 200) FROM "tabProgramEventLog";
SELECT * FROM "tabError Log" WHERE error::text LIKE '%foo%';

-- FAILS — `function left(json, integer) does not exist`
SELECT LEFT(details, 200) FROM "tabProgramEventLog";
SELECT * FROM "tabError Log" WHERE error LIKE '%foo%';

Affects ProgramEventLog.details, Submission.feedback, Error Log.error, and any column declared as Code (JSON) in DocType JSON. Lesson L-051.

docs.title: Frappe column-name surprises (no consistent mapping from field label to DB column)
docs.text:
DocType Field label / what you think it's called Real Postgres column Notes Error Log "Title" / what log_error(title=...) takes method The kwarg is title=, the column is method. Both are correct — Frappe maps title→method internally. Query with WHERE method LIKE 'SP %'. Error Log "Error" / "Message" / the long body error Not message. And it's JSON-typed (see above). ProgramEventLog The PE foreign key enrollment NOT program_enrollment despite the convention used elsewhere. Hit during 2026-05-26 diagnostics.

Rule: when raw SQL against a Frappe doctype errors with column "X" does not exist, do NOT assume the field is misnamed — check the actual schema first:

SELECT column_name FROM information_schema.columns
 WHERE table_name = 'tabError Log' AND table_schema = 'public'
 ORDER BY ordinal_position;

docs.title: A failed query poisons the transaction until you call frappe.db.rollback()
docs.text:
Unlike MariaDB (autocommits) PG enters an aborted-transaction state on the first failed statement. EVERY subsequent statement in the same txn errors with InFailedSqlTransaction: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block. Two implications:

  1. In bench console, wrap risky probes or start each cell with frappe.db.rollback(). The corollary is that sp_console helpers all begin with that call.
  2. In exception handlers that call frappe.log_error, rollback BEFORE log_error. frappe.log_error does its own SELECT to fetch the Error Log doctype meta; without the rollback that SELECT itself fails and you lose the entire error report.
try:
    frappe.db.sql("...risky SQL...")
except Exception as e:
    try:
        frappe.db.rollback()    # ← clear the poisoned txn FIRST
    except Exception:
        pass
    frappe.log_error(f"failed: {e}", "My App")    # now this actually works
    raise   # in an RQ job, ALWAYS re-raise (see frappe-hooks skill)

Lesson L-030. Documented in CLAUDE.md as a project-level gotcha.

docs.title: Console writes need an explicit frappe.db.commit() to persist
docs.text: IPython console runs everything in one implicit transaction. If a later cell errors and you call frappe.db.rollback(), all uncommitted writes from EARLIER cells (including frappe.log_error inserts and frappe.db.set_value updates) get wiped along with the poisoned txn. After diagnostics that depend on side effects (event log entries, prospect_id cache writes), call frappe.db.commit() before any subsequent query that could fail.

docs.title: Use the query builder when you can
docs.text:
frappe.qb (PyPika under the hood) emits dialect-correct SQL for both backends:

from frappe.query_builder import DocType
from frappe.query_builder.functions import Coalesce, Count

Enrollment = DocType("Course Enrollment")
Course = DocType("Course")

q = (
    frappe.qb.from_(Enrollment)
    .left_join(Course).on(Enrollment.course == Course.name)
    .select(Course.title, Count(Enrollment.name).as_("enrollments"))
    .where(Enrollment.status == "Active")
    .groupby(Course.title)
    .orderby(Count(Enrollment.name), order=frappe.qb.desc)
)
rows = q.run(as_dict=True)

This is the strongly-recommended default for non-trivial queries.

docs.title: Indexes
docs.text:
Frappe creates indexes on Link fields and on fields with index: 1 in the JSON. After adding index: 1, run bench migrate — Frappe will issue CREATE INDEX against PG.

For composite indexes or partial indexes (PG-only feature, very useful), use a patch:

# app/<your_app>/patches/v1_0/add_active_enrollment_index.py
import frappe

def execute():
    frappe.db.sql_ddl(
        'CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_active_enrollment '
        'ON "tabCourse Enrollment" (student, course) '
        'WHERE status = \'Active\';'
    )

Register the patch in app/<your_app>/patches.txt so bench migrate picks it up.

docs.title: Migrations & schema sync
docs.text:
bench migrate runs frappe.model.sync.sync_for("<app>") which diffs the DocType JSON against the live PG schema and issues ALTER TABLE statements. Watch for:

  • Renaming a field doesn't auto-rename the column. You need a patch that runs frappe.db.rename_column (or hand-rolled ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN).
  • Changing a field's fieldtype may require a USING clause for PG to coerce existing data. Frappe tries; sometimes you must intervene.
  • Dropping a field doesn't drop the column by default — Frappe leaves it for safety. Use DROP COLUMN in a patch if you really want it gone.

docs.title: Migration co-authoring — three artifacts must agree
docs.text:
When you add a new column to a doctype, three artifacts must be edited in the same change set. Edit two but not the third and bench migrate fails at the worst possible moment (production deploy, freshly cloned site, CI restore). The CR-005 PGCollection.kind incident shipped broken twice (2026-05-15) because of this exact mismatch.

Artifact What it controls <doctype>.json Whether the column exists in the schema after bench migrate Patch in patches/v0_X/*.py What backfill / SQL writes run against the new column patches.txt The ORDERING — whether the patch runs pre or post [post_model_sync]

docs.title: Hard rules
docs.text:
1. Every patch that references a new column should call frappe.reload_doc("<app>", "doctype", "<doctype>") at the top. This forces the DocType JSON to apply (creating the column if missing) BEFORE the patch body runs. Idempotent and cheap. See app/tap_lms/patches/v0_2/backfill_pg_collection_kinds.py and app/tap_lms/patches/v0_2/add_pe_glific_id_unique_index.py for the canonical pattern.

  2. frappe.db.rollback() at the very top of every patch. Clears any poisoned transaction state from earlier patches in the chain. Without this, a single upstream failure cascades through every subsequent patch with current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block.

  3. Use IF NOT EXISTS on every CREATE INDEX / CREATE TABLE. Patches are idempotent by Frappe convention (L-021) — re-running on a partially- migrated DB must be a no-op, never a "duplicate object" error.

docs.title: Canonical patch skeleton
docs.text:
"""
<purpose, 1-3 lines>
"""
import frappe


def execute():
    # PG txn hygiene — clear any poisoned txn state from prior patches.
    frappe.db.rollback()

    # Self-heal: force the doctype JSON to sync so columns we reference
    # are guaranteed live before our SQL runs. Idempotent + cheap.
    frappe.reload_doc("tap_lms", "doctype", "<doctype>")

    # Actual migration work — use IF NOT EXISTS for DDL idempotency.
    frappe.db.sql("""
        CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_foo
            ON "tabBar" (some_col)
         WHERE some_col IS NOT NULL
    """)
    frappe.db.commit()

    frappe.logger().info("patch_foo: ...")

docs.title: patches.txt — section headers are mandatory (L-058)
docs.text:
Frappe's patch loader uses configparser to read patches.txt and runs two distinct phases:

  1. pre_model_sync — patches that need to run BEFORE the doctype sync (rare; mostly for cleanup that the schema sync would otherwise stumble on)
  2. sync_doctypes() — creates/alters all doctype tables
  3. post_model_sync — patches that need to run AFTER the tables exist (the common case for tap_lms — every patch references SP doctype tables)

Required shape — both section headers, even if one is empty:

[pre_model_sync]

[post_model_sync]
tap_lms.patches.cr_004_scale.idx_pe_next_action
tap_lms.patches.cr_004_batch_id_unique.batch_id_unique_constraint
tap_lms.patches.v0_2.backfill_pg_collection_kinds
...

Common failure modes:

If patches.txt has... Frappe behavior No section headers at all All patches default to pre_model_sync → run BEFORE tables exist → fail with UndefinedTable on fresh installs Only [post_model_sync] Loader queries [pre_model_sync] first, can't find it → ValidationError: Patch type PatchType.pre_model_sync not found in patches.txt Only [pre_model_sync] Same as above but mirrored — fails when post_model_sync query happens Both headers, empty pre_model_sync ✅ Works Both headers populated correctly ✅ Works

We hit this on 2026-05-30 during the prod first-install. On migration deploys the bug is invisible because the tables already exist from earlier migrates; on fresh installs every patch fails.

docs.title: Patches reading from dropped legacy columns need has_column guards (L-059)
docs.text:
When a CR drops a column from a doctype's JSON AND the same CR includes a backfill patch that reads from that column for the migration path, the patch must guard the read:

def execute():
    # On migration deploys, the legacy column still exists in PG
    # (Frappe doesn't auto-drop columns when a field is removed from JSON).
    # On fresh installs, the column was never created.
    if frappe.db.has_column("tabEscalationStep", "message_type"):
        backfilled = frappe.db.sql("""
            UPDATE "tabEscalationStep"
               SET escalation_type = CASE
                       WHEN message_type = 'help_note_a' THEN 'help_note_a'
                       ...
                   END
             WHERE escalation_type IS NULL OR escalation_type = ''
            RETURNING name
        """)
        backfill_count = len(backfilled or [])
    else:
        backfill_count = 0   # fresh install — nothing to backfill

Without the guard, the patch fails on fresh installs with psycopg2.errors.UndefinedColumn: column "message_type" does not exist.

Hit 2026-05-30 in cr_003.per_week_grace_and_channels Step 1 against tabEscalationStep.message_type. The patch was unblocked by manually inserting a Patch Log entry (Step 1 was a no-op on the empty fresh table anyway); the source-tree fix added the guard.

docs.title: Reviewer rule
docs.text: When reviewing a new patch, verify: - [ ] frappe.db.rollback() at the top - [ ] frappe.reload_doc(...) if any column referenced is newly added - [ ] IF NOT EXISTS on all CREATE statements - [ ] Idempotent on re-run (no errors, no duplicate side effects) - [ ] Listed in patches.txt under [post_model_sync] (not above any header) - [ ] patches.txt has BOTH [pre_model_sync] and [post_model_sync] section headers (L-058) - [ ] Reads from LEGACY columns (being dropped in the same CR) are guarded with frappe.db.has_column(table, col) (L-059) - [ ] DocType JSON has the column the patch reads/writes — if not, the patch is shipping ahead of the schema and will fail on a fresh install

docs.title: Backups and restore
docs.text:
# Backup
bench --site <site> backup --with-files
# This produces SQL dumps via pg_dump under the hood.

# Manual backup of just the DB
pg_dump -U <db_user> -h 127.0.0.1 -d <db_name> -F c -f /tmp/site.dump

# Restore
pg_restore -U <db_user> -h 127.0.0.1 -d <db_name> --clean /tmp/site.dump

bench restore <sql_path> works for .sql.gz dumps produced by Frappe; if you've taken a custom pg_dump, restore with pg_restore directly.

docs.title: Connection tuning
docs.text:
In common_site_config.json:

{
  "db_type": "postgres",
  "db_host": "127.0.0.1",
  "db_port": 5432,
  "rds_db": 0
}

Per-site DB credentials in sites/<site>/site_config.json. Production: bump max_connections (PG default 100 is too low if you run multiple workers + gunicorn) and ensure shared_buffers is at least 25% of RAM.

docs.title: Locking
docs.text: Frappe acquires advisory locks via frappe.db.get_value(..., for_update=True) which translates to SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. Hold these locks for as little time as possible — in PG, a long-held row lock can block migrations and other writers.

docs.title: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for parallel workers
docs.text:
PG-specific (not in MariaDB until 8.0+, and even there with caveats). The right primitive for parallel scheduler tick handlers that want to grab the next batch without blocking on rows another worker already holds:

SELECT name, next_action_type, journey_label
  FROM "tabProgramEnrollment"
 WHERE next_action_at <= NOW()
   AND next_action_at IS NOT NULL
   AND program_status = 'active'
 ORDER BY next_action_at
 LIMIT 1000
 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Lesson L-003. See also pattern P-003 (per-PE event-driven scheduler tick) for the full shape.

docs.title: The atomic-claim pattern (project canonical)
docs.text:
Every state-changing UPDATE on ProgramEnrollment (or any state-machine doc) must include a WHERE journey_label = expected_label guard plus RETURNING name, and check the result. 0 rows returned = a parallel handler already moved the state, skip gracefully. This is the project's idempotency primitive — pattern P-001 in .claude/memory/patterns.md.

claimed = frappe.db.sql("""
    UPDATE "tabProgramEnrollment"
       SET resolved_flow_state = %s,
           journey_label       = %s,
           next_action_at      = %s,
           next_action_type    = %s
     WHERE name          = %s
       AND journey_label = %s         -- ← idempotency guard
     RETURNING name
""", (new_state, new_label, next_at, next_type, pe_name, expected_label))

if not claimed:
    return                    # parallel handler already moved state

Anti-patterns to flag in review:

  • A broad except Exception: block wrapping the UPDATE with a "MariaDB fallback" branch — that's dead code on this PG-only project, swallows real errors, and risks double-running. Remove it (lesson L-007).
  • SELECT ROW_COUNT() instead of RETURNING — see above, L-001.
  • Using pe = frappe.get_doc(...); pe.field += x; pe.save() for fields that race against scheduler resets — use the COALESCE-update form (pattern P-002) instead.

docs.title: Race-tolerant counter updates
docs.text:
For columns that can be reset (e.g., weekly_* fields T14 zeros out) or incremented from multiple handlers, never read-then-write. Use a single atomic UPDATE with COALESCE:

UPDATE "tabProgramEnrollment"
   SET total_quiz_points  = COALESCE(total_quiz_points, 0)  + %s,
       weekly_quiz_points = COALESCE(weekly_quiz_points, 0) + %s
 WHERE name = %s

Lesson L-011, pattern P-002.

docs.title: Vacuum and analyze
docs.text:
PG's autovacuum handles most cases, but after a big migration or bulk import, run VACUUM ANALYZE on the affected tables manually to refresh statistics. The query planner uses these stats; stale stats produce sequential scans on tables that have indexes.

psql -U <db_user> -d <db_name> -c 'VACUUM ANALYZE "tabCourse Enrollment";'

docs.title: Debugging slow queries
docs.text:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ... ;

Look for Seq Scan on big tables — usually means a missing index or a planner issue. PG has a richer EXPLAIN output than MariaDB; learn to read it.

docs.title: Don't reach for these
docs.text:
• Stored procedures and triggers in PG — Frappe's framework expects logic in Python controllers, not in the DB. You'll create maintenance pain and confuse the migration path.
  • pg_partman partitioning — works, but Frappe's ORM doesn't know about partitions and you'll get surprises in frappe.get_all.
  • Foreign key constraints beyond what Frappe creates — Frappe enforces relationships in Python, not at the DB level. Adding raw FKs can break delete operations.

docs.title: Frappe testing skill
docs.text: Frappe ships a unittest-based test runner that bootstraps a fully working site, runs your tests inside a transaction, and rolls back at the end. That last bit is what makes Frappe testing pleasant — every test starts from a clean DB.

docs.title: Tests are part of the feature, not a follow-up
docs.text:
This rule has been violated three times running. Codified now to stop the bleeding (L-025).

Hard rule: a function that touches Glific (start_contact_flow, start_group_flow, update_contact_fields), RabbitMQ (publish, consume), Google Cloud Storage, the database via raw SQL or frappe.db.set_value, or shared scheduler / cron state MUST ship with at least one test in the same commit as the function. Filing the test as a follow-up task (#21, #41, #53, …) is not acceptable. The bug always lands before the follow-up does, every time.

This applies to feature-builder handoffs and to code-reviewer's blocking criteria. See .claude/agents/feature-builder.md workflow step "After you finish" and .claude/agents/code-reviewer.md test-coverage section.

docs.title: What category of test applies — 5-line decision tree
docs.text:
1. Touches Glific or RabbitMQ or GCS? → unittest.mock mock + assert call shape AND a fault-injection test that raises and asserts retry/DLQ behavior (L-015).
  2. Atomic-claim or COALESCE-update SQL (P-001 / P-002)? → concurrency/race test calling the handler twice and asserting only one side-effect (L-018).
  3. Scheduler tick / cron path? → time-controlled test that runs the tick with frozen frappe.utils.now_datetime() and asserts dispatch idempotency.
  4. Whitelisted endpoint? → happy-path + validation-error + permission test (L-016).
  5. Pure CRUD on own DocType? → one happy-path test is enough; no race or mock needed.

If the function fits more than one row, it needs tests from each row.

Recurrence: missing_tests_on_new_api appeared 3x in .claude/memory/code-review-findings.jsonl (commits fca37df, 875d6d6, post-875d6d6). Commit 875d6d6 shipped 10+ new functions (pe_dispatcher 565 lines, 8 handlers, plus feedback_consumer_hook, _seed_pe_actions, check_auto_activate, staggered_action_time) with zero tests. The fix-up commit added 10 tests but left 5 handlers uncovered. The cost is one more BLOCKING review per missed function.

docs.title: Before moving / refactoring an existing function — check its failure history
docs.text:
Beyond the test-coverage checklist for new code, refactors of existing code need a pre-flight check. The pattern that hit us during the 2026-05-28 journey/ → summer_program/ migration: a function had silently-swallowed exceptions for days; the queue diagnostic showed 5 historical failures; the move was performed without investigating; the bug would have followed the file to the new location.

Hard rule for refactors that relocate or rename a function: before declaring the move "safe," grep its failure history:

# After loading sp_console (see skills/frappe-bench/SKILL.md console section):
queue_failures_for("the_function_name")

Plus the Error Log doctype:

import frappe; frappe.db.rollback()
frappe.db.sql("""
    SELECT method, creation, LEFT(error::text, 200) AS excerpt
      FROM "tabError Log"
     WHERE error::text LIKE %s
     ORDER BY creation DESC LIMIT 20
""", ("%the_function_name%",), as_dict=True)

If either query returns hits, the move becomes a refactor: fix the root cause inline (the fix-pattern usually already exists elsewhere in the codebase) BEFORE relocating the code. Don't migrate broken code unchanged; you'll ship the same bug to a new location and a reviewer will catch it later anyway.

This was L-057-proposed in the 2026-05-26 housekeeping retrospective.

docs.title: Where tests live
docs.text:
app/<your_app>/<your_module>/doctype/course_enrollment/test_course_enrollment.py
app/<your_app>/<your_module>/tests/test_<feature>.py

The test_ prefix is required — that's how the runner discovers them. One test file per DocType is conventional; cross-cutting features get their own tests/ folder.

docs.title: Anatomy
docs.text:
import frappe
import unittest

class TestCourseEnrollment(unittest.TestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        # Runs once before any test in this class. Use to seed reference data
        # the whole class shares. Not rolled back automatically — clean up in tearDownClass.
        cls.student = make_student("STU-TEST-001")
        cls.course = make_course("CS-TEST-101")

    def setUp(self):
        # Runs before each test. Frappe wraps each test in a transaction
        # that's rolled back, so most setUp work is unneeded.
        pass

    def test_creates_enrollment(self):
        doc = frappe.get_doc({
            "doctype": "Course Enrollment",
            "student": self.student,
            "course": self.course,
        }).insert()
        self.assertEqual(doc.status, "Active")
        self.assertTrue(frappe.db.exists("Course Enrollment", doc.name))

    def test_blocks_duplicate_enrollment(self):
        frappe.get_doc({
            "doctype": "Course Enrollment",
            "student": self.student,
            "course": self.course,
        }).insert()
        with self.assertRaises(frappe.ValidationError):
            frappe.get_doc({
                "doctype": "Course Enrollment",
                "student": self.student,
                "course": self.course,
            }).insert()

    @classmethod
    def tearDownClass(cls):
        # Clean up class-level seed data.
        for name in frappe.get_all("Course Enrollment", filters={"student": cls.student}, pluck="name"):
            frappe.delete_doc("Course Enrollment", name, force=True)

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
# All tests in your app
bench --site <site> run-tests --app tap_lms

# Single module
bench --site <site> run-tests --module tap_lms.tap_lms.doctype.course_enrollment.test_course_enrollment

# Single test
bench --site <site> run-tests --test tap_lms.tap_lms.doctype.course_enrollment.test_course_enrollment.TestCourseEnrollment.test_blocks_duplicate_enrollment

# With coverage
bench --site <site> run-tests --app tap_lms --coverage

Pass --profile to get per-test timing.

docs.title: Frappe's quality-of-life helpers
docs.text:
frappe.tests.utils.FrappeTestCase (subclass instead of unittest.TestCase) gives you:

  • self.assertDocumentEqual(expected_dict, doc) — compares meaningful fields.
  • Automatic transaction wrapping with rollback on every test.
  • A self.client for HTTP-style calls into your whitelisted methods.
from frappe.tests.utils import FrappeTestCase

class TestEnrollAPI(FrappeTestCase):
    def test_enroll_endpoint(self):
        result = frappe.call("tap_lms.api.enroll", student="STU-001", course="CS101")
        self.assertTrue(result["created"])

docs.title: Project test factories — use these, don't reinvent
docs.text:
The Summer Program has a canonical factory module at app/tap_lms/summer_program/tests/factories.py exposing:

  • make_batch(label, batch_id, ...) — populates EVERY mandatory field on the Batch doctype (start_date, end_date, regist_start_date, regist_end_date, batch_id, program_type, total_weeks, current_calendar_week, grace_window_days). Pass label (unique per test) and batch_id (the friendly identifier, distinct from the doc name).
  • make_student(suffix, phone_prefix, glific_id, ...) — populates name1, phone, glific_id, archetype, experiment_arm, language. Each test file should use a unique phone_prefix to keep its students in a disjoint phone space.
  • make_active_pe(student_id, batch_name, glific_id) — directly inserts a minimal active PE without running _process_pe_chunk. Useful for setting up pre-conditions like "sibling A is already enrolled."

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text:
Each test file inventing its own _ensure_batch() is the recurring mandatory_field_missing pattern (4× recurrence between 2026-05-16 and 2026-05-19). The Batch doctype gained regist_end_date as mandatory at some point; test files written before that change kept passing while new ones written without checking the doctype's mandatory list failed at setUpClass time.

When the doctype gains a new mandatory field, update factories.py once — every test that imports the factory inherits the fix. Test files that inline their own fixture have to be patched individually and inevitably one gets missed.

docs.title: Usage pattern
docs.text:
from tap_lms.summer_program.tests.factories import (
    make_batch, make_student, make_active_pe,
)

class TestMyFeature(FrappeTestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        super().setUpClass()
        cls.batch = make_batch("MyFeatureTestBatch", batch_id="MF01")

    def test_something(self):
        student = make_student(
            suffix="01",
            phone_prefix="+9999800",   # unique-per-test prefix
            glific_id="glific-mf-01",
        )
        pe = make_active_pe(student, self.batch, glific_id="glific-mf-01")
        # ... assertions

docs.title: Hard rule
docs.text:
Do not redefine _ensure_batch / _ensure_student / _ensure_pe in new test files. Import from factories.py. The reviewer treats local fixture inlining as a Major finding when the factory covers the case.

If you genuinely need a different fixture shape (e.g. a Batch with a specific program_type value the factory doesn't expose), pass it as a kwarg to the factory. If the factory doesn't accept that kwarg, ADD IT to the factory rather than inline a one-off.

docs.title: Generic test data factories (for new modules without their own)
docs.text:
Don't paste DocType creation everywhere — write factories.

# app/<your_app>/tests/factories.py
import frappe

def make_student(student_id="STU-AUTO", **overrides):
    if frappe.db.exists("Student", student_id):
        return student_id
    return frappe.get_doc({
        "doctype": "Student",
        "student_id": student_id,
        "first_name": overrides.get("first_name", "Test"),
        "last_name": overrides.get("last_name", "Student"),
        "email": overrides.get("email", f"{student_id.lower()}@test.local"),
    }).insert(ignore_permissions=True).name

def make_course(code="CS-AUTO", **overrides):
    if frappe.db.exists("Course", code):
        return code
    return frappe.get_doc({
        "doctype": "Course",
        "course_code": code,
        "title": overrides.get("title", f"Test Course {code}"),
        "credits": overrides.get("credits", 3),
    }).insert(ignore_permissions=True).name

docs.title: User context
docs.text:
Tests run as Administrator by default. To exercise permission logic:

def test_student_cannot_delete_enrollment(self):
    frappe.set_user("student@test.local")
    try:
        with self.assertRaises(frappe.PermissionError):
            frappe.delete_doc("Course Enrollment", self.enrollment)
    finally:
        frappe.set_user("Administrator")

Always restore Administrator in finally — leaks bleed across tests.

docs.title: Mocking external services
docs.text:
Frappe doesn't bundle a mocking library — use unittest.mock:

from unittest.mock import patch

def test_webhook_calls_payment_provider(self):
    with patch("tap_lms.tap_lms.payments.requests.post") as fake_post:
        fake_post.return_value.status_code = 200
        fake_post.return_value.json.return_value = {"ok": True}
        # ... call the code that hits the provider
        fake_post.assert_called_once()

For email, set frappe.flags.in_test = True (the test runner does this automatically) — emails are queued, not sent.

For background jobs, in tests they run synchronously by default unless frappe.flags.now = True is overridden. To assert a job was enqueued without running it, patch frappe.enqueue.

docs.title: What about pytest?
docs.text:
Frappe v15+ has experimental pytest support via pytest-frappe. The wins are richer fixtures, parallelism, and parameterization. The cost is one more dependency and slightly different conventions. Decision is yours; the unittest runner is fine for most cases. If you adopt pytest, fixtures replace setUpClass:

import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def student():
    return make_student("STU-PYTEST")

def test_enrollment_creates_progress(student):
    ...

docs.title: CI integration
docs.text:
A minimal GitHub Actions step:

- name: Set up bench (Postgres)
  run: |
    pip install frappe-bench
    bench init --frappe-branch version-15 frappe-bench --skip-redis-config-generation --skip-assets
    cd frappe-bench
    bench new-site test_site --db-type postgres --db-host 127.0.0.1 --admin-password admin
    bench --site test_site install-app tap_lms

- name: Run tests
  working-directory: frappe-bench
  run: bench --site test_site run-tests --app tap_lms --coverage

Pin the Frappe branch and Postgres version. Test environments diverging from prod is the leading cause of "passes locally, fails in CI."

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
• A test that calls frappe.db.commit() will break the rollback contract — every later test in the run sees the leaked data. Don't commit in tests.
  • A test that mutates the metadata cache (frappe.clear_cache() then loads new DocTypes) bleeds across tests. Reset what you mutate in tearDown.
  • Permission tests that don't restore the user (see above) cause "but it works on my machine" debugging hell.
  • Tests that assume autoincrement names (CRS-00001) are brittle — name your test fixtures explicitly.
  • Long test setup that creates 50 docs to test one thing — extract a factory; you'll thank yourself.

docs.title: When a feature ships
docs.text: Aim for: one happy path, one validation/edge-case, one permission test per public-facing controller method or whitelisted API. That's the minimum bar for "this is reviewed and tested" — anything less, the code-reviewer agent will flag (lesson L-016).

docs.title: Project-specific test rules
docs.text:
These rules come from real bugs that shipped and are non-negotiable:

  • Never call frappe.db.commit() in tests. The runner relies on transaction rollback for isolation. A single commit leaks data into every later test in the run. Lesson L-017. Code-reviewer flags this as BLOCKING.
  • Atomic-claim code needs an actual concurrency test. A SELECT ROW_COUNT() style PG-incompatibility bug cannot be caught by code review alone — it surfaces only when a duplicate UPDATE runs and the code can't tell the difference. Every state-changing UPDATE that uses pattern P-001 needs a test that:
  • Sets the doc to expected_label.
  • Calls the handler twice in the same test (or from two threads) and asserts the second call is a no-op (no double-side-effects, no exception).
  • Asserts the row's journey_label advanced exactly once.

Lesson L-018. Without this test, the bug ships. - Restore Administrator after permission tests. Always wrap frappe.set_user(...) in try/finally — leaks bleed across tests in the same run.
